title: Day 23 — plan and analyse a small biological study
text: Lecture slides · Weekly self-check

title: Day 23 — plan and analyse a small biological study
section: The question
text:
The question
Duckweed is a small aquatic plant that grows as floating fronds. In our simulated study, twenty separate flasks started with equal amounts of duckweed. Ten flasks were randomly allocated additional nutrients; ten were controls. Final dry biomass was measured after seven days. How does biomass differ between the two allocations, and how uncertain is that estimated difference?
This is guided practice, not an additional examination. Use the workflow you already know with a new dataset. Your deliverable is duckweed-report.Rmd, saved in the project root, and its rendered HTML. Keep the original CSV intact.
Complete one study, not two: use the duckweed study below, or choose the organic-laboratory alternative at the end of this page if your teacher selects that context. The alternative uses the same import/check/plot/report workflow and ends with a descriptive comparison; no new chemistry knowledge or test is required. It does not replace the guided statistical practice in week 4.

title: Day 23 — plan and analyse a small biological study
section: 1. Read the design before the numbers
text:
1. Read the design before the numbers
Open the data dictionary, then locate data/duckweed.csv. The columns are flask_id, treatment, and biomass_mg. The two allocation labels are control and nutrient. One nutrient flask, F17, was spilled before weighing, so its final biomass is unavailable.
In a few sentences, state the question, independent experimental unit, outcome and units, and what happened to F17. Fronds in one flask share their environment; counting them as separate independent replicates would misrepresent the design.
Before analysis, predict the kind of output needed: a plot showing flasks, a summary by group, and an estimate of nutrient minus control mean biomass with its confidence interval. You are not trying to make a p-value small.

title: Day 23 — plan and analyse a small biological study
section: 2. Make a report that runs from its own code
text:
2. Make a report that runs from its own code
Copy the starter report.Rmd using Save As, naming the copy duckweed-report.Rmd in the same project root. Replace the title and biological description. Remove seedling-specific chunks and interpretations before adding duckweed code. Load the same three packages in the setup chunk.
Begin with an import and inspection:
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
duckweed <- read_csv("data/duckweed.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
glimpse(duckweed)
Check row count, distinct identifiers, group labels, missing measurements, and the plausible range of biomass. Record checks as evidence, not simply “the data were checked”. Do not change the missing F17 value to zero or delete the entire row from your original input.






Hint: count missing and available measurements





Within group_by(treatment), use summarise() with n(), sum(!is.na(biomass_mg)), and sum(is.na(biomass_mg)). The number of rows and the number of usable measurements are different here. Use na.rm = TRUE for the mean and SD, while still reporting the missing count.

title: Day 23 — plan and analyse a small biological study
section: 3. Make the descriptive result first
text:
3. Make the descriptive result first
Create a group summary with available n, mean, and SD, all clearly labelled. Make a plot of individual biomass measurements by allocation, using only the available measurements for plotted y values. State how many are unavailable in the caption. A separate available object makes the exclusion explicit:
available <- duckweed |>
  filter(!is.na(biomass_mg))
Use the plot to ask whether the groups differ in location, how much overlap there is, and whether an observation needs checking against source records. No source evidence identifies another value as erroneous. Do not remove a value merely because it looks inconvenient.






Hint: adapt a familiar plot





Start with the week 3 individual-point plot. Change the data to available, x to treatment, y to biomass_mg, and the y-axis label to “Dry biomass after seven days (mg)”. Use horizontal jitter only, so vertical positions stay accurate.

title: Day 23 — plan and analyse a small biological study
section: 4. Estimate the difference
text:
4. Estimate the difference
Explain why an independent comparison is appropriate and why this is not a paired before/after analysis. Inspect the individual measurements for severe skew or an influential point; seek advice if the simple model appears unsuitable. Use the guided Welch approach from week 4. Extract nutrient and control vectors and give them in that order to t.test() so that the difference is nutrient minus control. The missing F17 measurement is absent from available, not replaced with an invented value.






Hint: preserve the stated comparison direction





nutrient <- available |>
  filter(treatment == "nutrient")
control <- available |>
  filter(treatment == "control")
comparison <- t.test(nutrient$biomass_mg, control$biomass_mg)
comparison
Read the two means and compute their difference explicitly. comparison$conf.int is the confidence interval for the difference in the order used above.

title: Day 23 — plan and analyse a small biological study
section: 5. Write the interpretation before polishing
text:
5. Write the interpretation before polishing
Use a short paragraph containing the observed direction and size of the difference in mg, the available sample sizes, the confidence interval, and the p-value with an explanation tied to the question. Add a limitation concerning the missing measurement and the conditions of this small simulated experiment.
Distinguish “these observations support a difference under this model” from “nutrients always produce this change in all plants”. If an interval includes zero, report the uncertainty; do not translate it into proof of no effect. Neither outcome needs rescuing by trying other tests.

title: Day 23 — plan and analyse a small biological study
section: Completion check
text:
Completion check

Could a reader identify the flask as the independent unit without opening code?
Are measurements missing for 1 flask, with 19 available in total?
Does the plot show observations and units, and explain the missing value?
Does the direction of the reported difference agree with the code and means?
Does every object used in the report originate in its chunks?







Self-check answers that do not depend on your conclusion





There are 20 rows and unique flask IDs. Ten control and nine nutrient flasks have biomass measurements. F17 remains a documented missing value. A positive nutrient-minus-control estimate means greater mean biomass in nutrient flasks. The conclusion still depends on design, assumptions, uncertainty, and context.

title: Day 23 — plan and analyse a small biological study
section: Alternative study: product yield in an organic laboratory
text:
Alternative study: product yield in an organic laboratory
Question: how does the percentage of product collected vary among the supplied runs and between two labelled protocols? Use this study instead of the duckweed report. Save organic-study.Rmd and its HTML at the project root. If you made organic-report.Rmd on day 15, keep that earlier work and use Save As to create organic-study.Rmd for this study.
An organic synthesis is a procedure intended to make a chemical product. For this exercise, the maximum possible product mass, called the theoretical mass, is already supplied; you do not need a reaction equation or to calculate it. Isolated mass is the dry product collected. Assume it is pure solely for this calculation. Define percentage yield by the supplied relationship:
yield (%) = 100 × isolated mass (g) / theoretical mass (g)
The file data/organic-recovery.csv contains 12 simulated independent synthesis runs, six randomly allocated standard and six modified protocol labels. The starting scales differ, so theoretical masses differ. Compare yields in percent, rather than comparing grams without accounting for those scales. All measurements are present. Repeated weighings of one collected product would not create new synthesis runs.
Start from a root-level copy of the template and remove the seedling-specific code and prose. Import and derive the outcome:
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
organic <- read_csv("data/organic-recovery.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
organic <- organic |>
  mutate(yield_percent = 100 * isolated_mass_g / theoretical_mass_g)

Check the 12 unique run_id values, six rows per protocol, numeric mass columns, no missing values, and positive theoretical masses. Check Y01 by hand: 0.62 g collected from a supplied 1.00 g maximum gives 62%.
Summarise n, mean, and SD of yield_percent by protocol. Label SD in percentage points, since it describes spread on a percent scale.
Plot individual yields by protocol with horizontal jitter only. Each point is an independent synthesis run. Save one summary CSV and one labelled PNG in output/, using names beginning organic-.
Describe the observed group difference and overlap. Report it in percentage points, defined as the modified mean minus the standard mean. No hypothesis test or confidence interval is required for this descriptive alternative.
Explain why higher yield alone does not establish greater purity, safety, sustainability, or general superiority. The simplified purity assumption is not an experimental verification of purity.
Render in a fresh R session. The report should identify its question, supplied theoretical masses, formula, independent units, units, checks, and limits.







Hint and completion checks for the alternative





Reuse group_by(protocol) and summarise(n = n(), mean_yield_percent = mean(yield_percent), sd_percentage_points = sd(yield_percent), .groups = "drop"). There are six available runs per protocol. The standard mean is about 68.67% and the modified mean about 77.00%, a descriptive difference of 8.33 percentage points. Do not call that an 8.33% relative increase, and do not claim an inferential conclusion from these summaries alone.



Before you finish: save a first rendered report and a note of anything that failed. Tomorrow we will test whether someone else can reproduce it: Day 24.

Does exit delete the files you saved remotely?

title: Day 20 — A biological association
text: Lecture slides · Weekly self-check

title: Day 20 — A biological association
section: Today’s question
text:
Today’s question
Do larger leaves tend to have greater dry mass? We now fit a line to observations of different plants, rather than prepared calibration standards. The R function is familiar, but the biological interpretation changes. A relationship between two measurements does not by itself establish that changing one causes the other.
data/leaf-mass.csv contains simulated data from one sampled leaf on each of 18 independent plants. leaf_area_cm2 measures area and dry_mass_mg measures mass after drying. The study is observational: leaf area was not randomly assigned. Species, age, environment, and other features could influence both measurements. We begin with the simple question about association within the observed range.

title: Day 20 — A biological association
section: Plot first, then fit
text:
Plot first, then fit

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

leaves <- read_csv("data/leaf-mass.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
leaf_plot <- ggplot(leaves, aes(x = leaf_area_cm2, y = dry_mass_mg)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  labs(x = "Leaf area (cm²)", y = "Leaf dry mass (mg)") +
  theme_minimal()
leaf_plot

leaf_fit <- lm(dry_mass_mg ~ leaf_area_cm2, data = leaves)
coef(leaf_fit)

Read the formula aloud: explain dry mass using leaf area. The fitted intercept is about 9.48 mg and slope about 4.11 mg/cm². In these observations, a one cm² difference in leaf area is associated with a fitted mean difference of about 4.11 mg in dry mass. The line summarises a tendency, not a fixed ratio that every leaf obeys.

leaf_plot <- leaf_plot +
  geom_abline(intercept = coef(leaf_fit)[1], slope = coef(leaf_fit)[2],
              colour = "steelblue")
leaf_plot
range(leaves$leaf_area_cm2)




One leaf from each of eighteen plants, with the fitted dry-mass relationship.


The observed areas range from 2.96 to 14.68 cm². An intercept is mathematically the fitted mass at zero area, but zero lies outside our data. Do not claim that a leaf with no area biologically weighs 9.48 mg. The fitted intercept helps position a line over the observed range.

title: Day 20 — A biological association
section: A line leaves individual differences
text:
A line leaves individual differences

leaves <- leaves |>
  mutate(fitted_mass_mg = fitted(leaf_fit),
         residual_mg = residuals(leaf_fit))

leaf_residual_plot <- ggplot(leaves, aes(x = leaf_area_cm2, y = residual_mg)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  labs(x = "Leaf area (cm²)", y = "Observed − fitted mass (mg)") +
  theme_minimal()
leaf_residual_plot




Individual dry-mass residuals around the leaf-area relationship.


Describe the residual pattern in ordinary language. Are points on both sides of zero? Is there obvious curvature? Does spread appear much greater at one end? These checks help identify limitations; they are not proof that every model assumption is satisfied. Independence still comes from how the plants were sampled, not from the residual plot.
Unusual points can influence the line, especially near the ends of the area range. We can explore that influence without deleting data from the main analysis:

without_a18 <- leaves |> filter(plant_id != "A18")
sensitivity_fit <- lm(dry_mass_mg ~ leaf_area_cm2, data = without_a18)
coef(leaf_fit)
coef(sensitivity_fit)

This is a demonstration, not a search for the slope we prefer. A18 has no known recording error and belongs in the main result. Compare the slopes and note whether omitting it changes the broad description. Never select observations according to which omission gives the smallest p-value.

title: Day 20 — A biological association
section: Keep prediction within the evidence
text:
Keep prediction within the evidence
For an area of 8 cm², calculate the fitted mean mass using the line:

coef(leaf_fit)[1] + coef(leaf_fit)[2] * 8

The result is about 42.36 mg. It is a fitted mean, not a promise that the next leaf will have that mass. There is individual variation around the line and uncertainty in the line itself. An area of 80 cm² is far outside the measured range; extrapolating there would rely on an untested assumption that the same relationship continues.

title: Day 20 — A biological association
section: Practical: choose an analysis for a question
text:
Practical: choose an analysis for a question
Create association-report.Rmd at the project root. Include the study design, point plot with fitted line, residual plot, slope interpretation with units, and observed range. Add a short sensitivity note explaining what the A18 exercise showed, while retaining all observations in the main model. Save the main figure as output/day20-leaf-line.png and render the report.
Finish with three sentences that answer different questions:

What association did we observe?
What does the fitted slope mean numerically and biologically?
What causal claim would this design fail to establish?

Then compare your reports from days 17 and 19. A two-group treatment question motivated a comparison of means; a concentration measurement motivated a calibration line; today’s two measured variables motivate an association. The biological question and design come before the choice of R function.






Hint: a precise slope sentence





Use “Within the observed area range, an additional 1 cm² of leaf area was associated with approximately … mg greater fitted mean dry mass.” Avoid “making the leaf larger causes …”, because this study did not manipulate area.

title: Day 20 — A biological association
section: Check your understanding
text:
Check your understanding

Is the slope measured in mg, cm², or mg/cm²? mg/cm².
Does a strong relationship establish causation? No.
Would 18 leaves from one plant provide the same independent sample as 18 plants? No; leaves sharing a plant may be dependent.

Leave with: a rendered association report and a clear explanation of how its question differs from a treatment comparison or instrument calibration.

title: Day 18 — The same plant measured twice
text: Lecture slides · Weekly self-check

title: Day 18 — The same plant measured twice
section: Today’s question
text:
Today’s question
Ten plants had their leaf photosynthesis measured before and after changing the light conditions. Did their measurements tend to increase? Every plant appears twice, so this is a paired design. We compare changes within plants rather than pretending that the two sets of readings came from different plants.
The file data/paired.csv contains simulated measurements in micromoles of CO2 per square metre per second, written µmol m⁻² s⁻¹. You do not need the chemistry to analyse this example: each number measures a rate, and higher means a greater rate of photosynthesis. Before and after were always measured in that order. That matters for our eventual interpretation.

title: Day 18 — The same plant measured twice
section: Each row keeps a pair together
text:
Each row keeps a pair together

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

paired <- read_csv("data/paired.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
paired
anyDuplicated(paired$plant_id)

There should be ten rows and no duplicate identifiers; anyDuplicated() returns zero when it finds none. Each row contains one plant’s before and after values. The identifiers tell us which measurements belong together. If measurements came in two files, we would need to match them by identifier before subtracting. The fact that two files each contain ten rows would not be sufficient.
Never sort the before values and after values independently. That would change which values are paired and manufacture different biological changes. Sorting the complete table by plant identifier is safe because whole rows move together.

title: Day 18 — The same plant measured twice
section: Make one change value per plant
text:
Make one change value per plant

paired <- paired |>
  mutate(change_umol_m2_s = after_umol_m2_s - before_umol_m2_s)

paired |>
  select(plant_id, before_umol_m2_s, after_umol_m2_s, change_umol_m2_s)

mean(paired$change_umol_m2_s)

Plant L01 changed from 5.87 to 6.95, an increase of 1.08 units. The mean of all ten changes is 1.983 units. Some plants start higher than others; analysing the within-plant changes recognises that each plant is its own reference.

change_plot <- ggplot(paired, aes(x = plant_id, y = change_umol_m2_s)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  labs(x = "Plant identifier", y = "After − before (µmol m⁻² s⁻¹)") +
  theme_minimal()
change_plot




Each point is one plant’s after-minus-before change; the dashed line marks no change.


The zero line means no change. This plot makes the paired comparison visible without requiring another data-reshaping tool. Inspect the changes, including the larger change for L02; a valid large change must not be removed merely because it is inconvenient.

title: Day 18 — The same plant measured twice
section: A paired t-test asks about the mean change
text:
A paired t-test asks about the mean change

paired_comparison <- t.test(paired$after_umol_m2_s,
                            paired$before_umol_m2_s,
                            paired = TRUE,
                            alternative = "two.sided")
paired_comparison

Here the first vector is after and the second before. The mean difference is therefore after minus before. The estimated mean change is about 1.98, with a 95% confidence interval from 1.25 to 2.71 units and p about 0.00017. The method describes uncertainty in the mean change, not the spread of individual changes. Its independent observations are the ten plants’ changes.
A paired t-test can also be understood as a one-sample t-test of the change values against zero. Try the following only after you can explain the first version; it should give the same estimated change, interval, and p-value:

t.test(paired$change_umol_m2_s, mu = 0)

title: Day 18 — The same plant measured twice
section: What this experiment can and cannot show
text:
What this experiment can and cannot show
The readings increased in this simulated dataset. But light condition and measurement order changed together. Time, acclimation, or equipment drift could also contribute. A small p-value does not untangle these possibilities. We can describe a before–after association and propose a better experiment, such as an appropriate control group and a design that addresses order effects.
This illustrates two different questions: are the observed changes consistent with a zero mean change, and what caused any change? A test addresses the first under assumptions; the experimental design determines what we can say about the second.

title: Day 18 — The same plant measured twice
section: Practical: a short paired report
text:
Practical: a short paired report
Copy the root report template to paired-report.Rmd at the project root. Include:

The question, units, and ten independent plants measured twice.
An import and ID check, the change calculation, and the change plot.
The paired t-test and an interpretation in the stated after-minus-before direction.
One sentence distinguishing the confidence interval from individual spread.
A limitation about order and an idea for improving the design.

Save change_plot as output/day18-changes.png and render the HTML. All the measurements are complete here. In real paired data, do not remove missing before and after values independently, since that can misalign the remaining pairs. Keep rows together and account for any incomplete pairs explicitly.






Hint: check the direction with one plant





Before trusting the test output, subtract L01’s before value from its after value. It should be positive 1.08. The same order belongs in both the change calculation and the two vectors supplied to t.test().

title: Day 18 — The same plant measured twice
section: Check your understanding
text:
Check your understanding

How many independent units are present? Ten plants, not twenty readings.
Would pairing unrelated plants by their row position be meaningful? No.
Does a small p-value establish that light caused the change? No; the fixed measurement order remains a limitation.

Leave with: paired-report.Rmd, its HTML, and the change figure.

title: Day 16 — What does a difference between groups mean?
text: Lecture slides · Weekly self-check

title: Day 16 — What does a difference between groups mean?
section: Today’s question
text:
Today’s question
Does the treatment change how much a seedling grows? We already know how to describe the plants we measured. Today we distinguish a difference in our sample from evidence about a wider process. We begin with plants and pictures, then add statistical language. No new test is needed today.
Open introcomputing.Rproj. Use the clean, simulated data/seedlings.csv, not your data-repair exercise. Each row is one independently potted plant. Twelve plants were randomly assigned to each group and measured before and after the same growth period. The outcome is growth in millimetres. The treatment label describes an experimental condition; these teaching data do not establish a claim about any actual product or organism.

title: Day 16 — What does a difference between groups mean?
section: Start with the question and the independent unit
text:
Start with the question and the independent unit
Our comparison is mean growth in treated plants minus mean growth in control plants. State that direction now: a positive difference means greater growth in the treated group. Keep it the same in your code and report.
The independent experimental unit is a plant in its own pot. Measuring one plant three times with a ruler may improve the measurement; it does not create three independent plants. Similarly, the initial and final measurements belong to the same plant. We subtract them to obtain one growth value per plant, then compare growth between the two independent treatment groups.

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

seedlings <- read_csv("data/seedlings.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
seedlings <- seedlings |>
  mutate(growth_mm = final_mm - initial_mm)

group_summary <- seedlings |>
  group_by(treatment) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean_growth_mm = mean(growth_mm),
            sd_growth_mm = sd(growth_mm), .groups = "drop")
group_summary

The control mean is about 15.28 mm; the treated mean is about 21.49 mm. Both groups contain 12 plants. Their observed difference is about 6.22 mm. A difference is a number with units, not merely a label such as “significant”.

title: Day 16 — What does a difference between groups mean?
section: Show the observations before summarising the evidence
text:
Show the observations before summarising the evidence

growth_plot <- ggplot(seedlings, aes(x = treatment, y = growth_mm)) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = 0.08, height = 0, seed = 16)) +
  labs(x = "Treatment group", y = "Growth over the study period (mm)") +
  theme_minimal()
growth_plot




Individual growth values in the supplied simulated dataset. The slight horizontal displacement separates overlapping dots.


The small horizontal displacement separates overlapping dots. It does not change their heights. You can see variation among individuals and overlap between the groups. Overlap does not automatically mean that the group means are equal; separated means do not mean that every treated plant grew more than every control plant. Compare both statements against the picture.

title: Day 16 — What does a difference between groups mean?
section: A sample difference is not the whole story
text:
A sample difference is not the whole story
If we repeated the experiment with another set of plants, we would get another difference. Random variation can produce unequal sample means even when the underlying group means are equal. Tomorrow’s test asks whether the observed difference is difficult to reconcile with a particular equal-means model.
The null hypothesis for this exercise is that the population mean growth is the same under the two conditions. A two-sided alternative allows a difference in either direction. We choose a two-sided question before looking for the most favourable result.
A p-value describes how often a result at least as extreme as the one observed would arise under the null model and its assumptions. For the t-test, “extreme” refers to the test statistic, which compares the mean difference with its estimated sampling uncertainty. A p-value is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true, and it does not measure the biological importance of a difference.

title: Day 16 — What does a difference between groups mean?
section: Practical: prepare a comparison report
text:
Practical: prepare a comparison report
Save a copy of the root-level report.Rmd as comparison.Rmd, also at the project root so its data/ paths work. Keep your earlier reports. In this new file:

Write the biological question, outcome units, and independent experimental unit.
Add the import, growth calculation, group summary, and individual-point plot.
Calculate the treated-minus-control difference with the following explicit extraction. pull() takes one column out of a table as a vector.


treated <- seedlings |>
  filter(treatment == "treated") |>
  pull(growth_mm)
control <- seedlings |>
  filter(treatment == "control") |>
  pull(growth_mm)

observed_difference <- mean(treated) - mean(control)
observed_difference


Write two sentences: one describes the sample difference, and one says what still remains uncertain about the wider population.
Save the figure with ggsave("output/day16-growth.png", growth_plot,    width = 6, height = 4) and render the report to HTML.







Hint: check a surprising sign





Read mean(treated) and mean(control) separately. The order in a subtraction matters. A negative result from mean(control) - mean(treated) would describe the reverse comparison, not a contradictory biological result.

title: Day 16 — What does a difference between groups mean?
section: Check your understanding
text:
Check your understanding

Can we conclude that every treated plant grew more? No; look at the dots.
Are 12 plants each measured twice 24 independent replicates per group? No; repeated measurements stay attached to their plant.
Does an observed mean difference alone tell us its sampling uncertainty? No; variability and sample size matter as well.

Leave with: comparison.Rmd, its rendered HTML, and output/day16-growth.png. Your report should currently describe the observations without pretending that a test has already been performed.

title: Day 15 — Describe the experiment without overstating it
section: Today’s question
text:
Today’s question
Can a reader understand the seedling measurements, their variation, and the limits of our description? A useful biological report does not need a significance test on every page. Today you will make the data handling, figure, summary, and interpretation fit together.
Save a new source document, descriptive-report.Rmd, at the project root. You may copy your first report’s structure, but deliberately revise its methods and interpretation. Keep data/ paths relative to this root. The supplied measurements are simulated. Plants received a control or nutrient treatment and were measured seven days apart; the nutrient formulation is unspecified.
Produce one descriptive report today. The teacher may choose the organic laboratory alternative below instead of the seedling report. In that case save organic-report.Rmd at the same project root and use its stated variables and units throughout; do not mix the two datasets in one set of results.

title: Day 15 — Describe the experiment without overstating it
section: Choose and state which input you use
text:
Choose and state which input you use
Use data/seedlings.csv for the core report. It contains 24 complete plant records. Include a data-quality note explaining the checks you performed: unique plant IDs, allowed treatment labels, numeric length columns, and missing-value counts. A statement that “R loaded the file” is not a data-quality check.
If the teacher asks you to report the repaired day 11 data instead, include the repair code or source it from a saved script within the project. Do not read a derived file that cannot be recreated from the shared raw data. State which source you used and retain the unavailable P06 observation; do not silently mix results from the repaired and complete datasets.

title: Day 15 — Describe the experiment without overstating it
section: Build the report in a clear order
text:
Build the report in a clear order
Use this order inside the report:

Load packages and import the input file.
Inspect its structure and document relevant data checks.
Derive growth_mm = final_mm - initial_mm.
Calculate the grouped summary with sample counts, mean, median, and SD.
Draw the individual-plant figure with group means.
Explain the centre, spread, overlap, and limitations in ordinary language.

Here is a compact data-check block that can appear after import:

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
seedlings <- read_csv("data/seedlings.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
anyDuplicated(seedlings$plant_id)
seedlings |> count(treatment)
sum(is.na(seedlings$initial_mm))
sum(is.na(seedlings$final_mm))
seedlings <- mutate(seedlings, growth_mm = final_mm - initial_mm)

anyDuplicated() returns zero when it finds no duplicate; a positive result identifies the position of the first duplicate, not a count of duplicates. Include only checking output that helps the reader, but keep the code available in the source. Reuse your day 13 summary and figure rather than replacing them with a screenshot of the RStudio Environment pane.
A table in an R Markdown chunk can be displayed neatly with:

group_summary <- seedlings |>
  group_by(treatment) |>
  summarise(n_observed = sum(!is.na(growth_mm)),
            mean_mm = mean(growth_mm, na.rm = TRUE),
            median_mm = median(growth_mm, na.rm = TRUE),
            sd_mm = sd(growth_mm, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")
knitr::kable(group_summary, digits = 2,
             caption = "Observed growth and variation by treatment; lengths in mm.")

The table is generated from code. If the data change, the rendered table can change too. A caption must distinguish SD among plants from uncertainty in the mean. This report has SD, not confidence intervals.

title: Day 15 — Describe the experiment without overstating it
section: Write with the question in view
text:
Write with the question in view
A useful description distinguishes three ideas: group averages differ in this sample; plants vary within each group; and sample descriptions do not quantify all uncertainty about a treatment effect. You can report observed values with units and identify the independent unit without declaring a universal result.
For the complete data, the group means are about 15.3 mm for controls and 21.5 mm for treated plants. Check your table rather than copying these numbers into prose without verification. The treated group also has more spread in these data. Do not say that every treated plant outgrew every control plant: the individual observations overlap.

title: Day 15 — Describe the experiment without overstating it
section: Alternative context: report collected-product yield
text:
Alternative context: report collected-product yield
Use this in place of the seedling report if selected. The question is: what percentage of the supplied maximum product mass was collected in each run, and how does it vary between protocols? All data are simulated. A synthesis run is one independently carried-out product-making experiment. Twelve independent runs were randomly assigned to two protocols, six to each. A protocol is a specified method; no knowledge of its chemical steps is required here.
theoretical_mass_g is the supplied maximum possible product mass for that run’s starting amounts. isolated_mass_g is the dry collected product mass, assumed pure for this simplified calculation. Both are in grams. Calculate percentage yield with 100 * isolated_mass_g / theoretical_mass_g, so Y01 is 100 * 0.62 / 1.00 = 62%. Theoretical masses differ with starting scale; compare the percentages, not the raw masses. You do not need to balance a reaction or calculate a theoretical mass yourself.

organic <- read_csv("data/organic-recovery.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(yield_percent = 100 * isolated_mass_g / theoretical_mass_g)
organic_summary <- organic |>
  group_by(protocol) |>
  summarise(n_runs = n(), mean_yield_percent = mean(yield_percent),
            sd_percentage_points = sd(yield_percent), .groups = "drop")
organic_summary

Follow the same report order: import and check IDs, labels, numeric masses, missing values, and positive theoretical masses; calculate yield; show a table and individual-run plot; then interpret centre, spread, and overlap. Both groups have six available runs. Mean yields are about 68.67% and 77.00%; SDs are about 4.32 and 3.74 percentage points for standard and modified protocols. Label the y-axis “Isolated product yield (%)” and identify one point as one run. Do not call repeated weighings of one product batch independent runs.
This is descriptive work: no t-test is needed. A higher mean yield does not establish greater purity, safety, environmental benefit, or superiority in other reactions. Write a limitation tied to the small simulated set and the assumed purity. Keep the source and data together so the report can render from scratch.

title: Day 15 — Describe the experiment without overstating it
section: Your practical and a reader check
text:
Your practical and a reader check

Complete the report with a question, data/design paragraph, methods, table, figure, and interpretation. Keep it short enough that each part earns its place.
Include the number of independent plants, or independent synthesis runs for the alternative, and state what the figure’s symbols represent. Name any exclusions or missing measurements.
Restart R and run this command in the R Console, not in a code chunk inside the report (a report must not try to render itself):


rmarkdown::render("descriptive-report.Rmd", output_dir = "reports")

For the organic alternative, replace the quoted filename with "organic-report.Rmd"; render only the report you chose.

Ask a partner to read the HTML. Can they identify the units, input file, observational unit, main pattern, and main limitation without opening RStudio?
If remote R access is available, locate the project on that computer and repeat the render there using the supplied connection instructions. First identify whether the R session and data are local or remote. Otherwise, repeat from a newly opened local project; do not invent connection details.







Hint: reproducibility is a file relationship





An HTML file beside an .Rmd is not enough if the source expects data in your personal Downloads folder. Keep the documented project structure, original data, and source together. The fresh-session render reveals missing dependencies.

title: Day 15 — Describe the experiment without overstating it
section: Check your understanding
text:
Check your understanding






A good limitation is specific





“The sample is small” is less informative than naming the independent unit, noting overlap or variation, and explaining that today’s report describes the sample without yet estimating uncertainty in a treatment difference. Missing observations, when present, should also be counted and discussed.



Keep: your chosen descriptive-report.Rmd or organic-report.Rmd and its HTML, with the code and data needed to render it. Next: from description to a comparison.

title: Day 13 — Summarise groups without hiding the plants
text: Lecture slides · Weekly self-check

title: Day 13 — Summarise groups without hiding the plants
section: Today’s question
text:
Today’s question
How can a figure and a small table show both the typical growth and differences among individual plants? A pair of bars showing only means would conceal sample size, spread, unusual observations, and overlap. We will show the observations and use summary numbers as an additional description.
Start day13-groups.R at the project root:

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
seedlings <- read_csv("data/seedlings.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(growth_mm = final_mm - initial_mm)

title: Day 13 — Summarise groups without hiding the plants
section: One row per group in a summary
text:
One row per group in a summary

group_summary <- seedlings |>
  group_by(treatment) |>
  summarise(n_plants = n(),
            n_observed = sum(!is.na(growth_mm)),
            mean_mm = mean(growth_mm, na.rm = TRUE),
            median_mm = median(growth_mm, na.rm = TRUE),
            sd_mm = sd(growth_mm, na.rm = TRUE),
            .groups = "drop")
group_summary

group_by(treatment) tells the next operation to work separately within each treatment. summarise() returns one row of results per group. The names on the left of = become output column names. n() counts rows; sum(!is.na(...)) counts observed measurements. Here ! means “not”, so the expression identifies values that are not missing. .groups = "drop" makes the resulting summary an ordinary ungrouped table.
This clean dataset has twelve observed growth values per group. The means are about 15.3 and 21.5 mm, and SDs about 3.19 and 4.87 mm for control and treated plants, respectively. The table is a different object from seedlings: group_summary contains two rows describing groups, not two newly measured plants.

title: Day 13 — Summarise groups without hiding the plants
section: Add a clearly identified mean
text:
Add a clearly identified mean

group_plot <- ggplot(seedlings, aes(x = treatment, y = growth_mm)) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = 0.08, height = 0, seed = 13),
             alpha = 0.75) +
  geom_point(data = group_summary, aes(x = treatment, y = mean_mm),
             inherit.aes = FALSE, shape = 18, size = 4, colour = "darkred") +
  labs(x = "Treatment", y = "Change in seedling length (mm)",
       caption = "Small dots: individual plants. Red diamonds: group means.") +
  theme_minimal()
group_plot

The second point layer uses the summary table. Its inherit.aes = FALSE means we supply its mappings explicitly instead of inheriting a column absent from that table. You can reuse this worked pattern; understanding the two tables matters more than memorising the option today.
If adding error bars, name exactly what they represent. Mean ± SD describes spread among observations. A confidence interval describes uncertainty in an estimated mean; the two are not interchangeable. It is fine to keep today’s figure as observations and means only.

title: Day 13 — Summarise groups without hiding the plants
section: A histogram answers a different question
text:
A histogram answers a different question

ggplot(seedlings, aes(x = growth_mm)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 4, boundary = 0, colour = "white") +
  facet_wrap(~ treatment, ncol = 1) +
  labs(x = "Change in seedling length (mm)", y = "Number of plants") +
  theme_minimal()

A histogram groups nearby numeric measurements into intervals, or bins. It shows a rough distribution, not the order in which plants were measured. With only twelve observations per group, its shape changes noticeably with the bin width. facet_wrap() gives a separate panel per treatment. Shared scales help compare the panels; small samples warrant cautious descriptions.

section: Your practical

Your practical

Save the table as output/growth-summary.csv and the plot as output/growth-summary.png, using write_csv() and ggsave().

If you completed day 11, summarise output/seedlings-cleaned.csv. Check the distinction between n_plants and n_observed. Explain why its control mean need not exactly match the complete clean teaching dataset’s mean. If the teacher selects the organic transfer below instead, substitute it for this step rather than adding a second analysis.

title: Day 13 — Summarise groups without hiding the plants
section: Transfer choice: summarise product yield
text:
Transfer choice: summarise product yield
In data/organic-recovery.csv, one row is one independently carried-out product-making experiment, or synthesis run. The supplied theoretical_mass_g is its maximum possible product mass; isolated_mass_g is dry collected product, assumed pure for this simplified exercise. Both are in grams. Derive yield_percent = 100 * isolated_mass_g / theoretical_mass_g; the first run is 100 * 0.62 / 1.00 = 62%. No chemical reaction calculation is required.
Import the file, derive yield, then adapt today’s grouped-summary pattern to group by protocol. Report the number of runs, mean percentage yield, and SD in percentage points. Adapt the individual-point plot to show yield by protocol. Do not plot group summaries as though they were individual runs. Save output/organic-yield-summary.csv, output/organic-yield-summary.png, and its caption instead of the extra cleaned-seedling summary.






Hint: keep the denominator and the experimental unit





Use mutate(yield_percent = 100 * isolated_mass_g / theoretical_mass_g), then group_by(protocol) and summarise(). Both groups have six independent runs. The standard mean is about 68.67% and the modified mean is 77.00%; show the individual values before interpreting the difference. Different starting scales mean that comparing raw grams would answer a different question.









Hint: keep object roles clear





write_csv(group_summary, "output/growth-summary.csv") saves the summary, while ggsave("output/growth-summary.png", plot = group_plot, width = 6, height = 4) saves the plot. These outputs have different purposes. Check names() if a layer mentions a column absent from the table used by that layer.

title: Day 13 — Summarise groups without hiding the plants
section: Check your understanding
text:
Check your understanding






Why show individual dots?





Dots reveal how many observations overlap, where unusual values lie, and how measurements vary around each mean. A higher mean does not mean every treated plant grew more than every control plant. The repaired dataset retains twelve control plants but only eleven observed control growth values.



Keep: day13-groups.R, the summary CSV, figure, and caption. Next: replicates and uncertainty.

title: Day 11 — Check the table before trusting the answer
text: Lecture slides · Weekly self-check

title: Day 11 — Check the table before trusting the answer
section: Today’s question
text:
Today’s question
What if a length was entered in the wrong unit, a plant appears twice, or a measurement is missing? R can calculate a precise-looking answer from a poor table. Our job is to check what the values mean and leave a record of justified repairs. Never edit the supplied raw file to make a calculation look convenient.
Today’s data/seedlings-messy.csv contains deliberately planted errors. Read data/field-notes.txt, which provides the source-record information needed to resolve them. This is a teaching exercise in verification, not a rule that unusual observations must be wrong.

title: Day 11 — Check the table before trusting the answer
section: Inspect before converting
text:
Inspect before converting
Create day11-cleaning.R in the project root. Read every column as text so that mixed entries remain visible. Keep leading/trailing spaces for this inspection.

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
raw <- read_csv("data/seedlings-messy.csv", show_col_types = FALSE,
                col_types = cols(.default = col_character()), trim_ws = FALSE)
dim(raw)
unique(raw$treatment)
filter(raw, plant_id %in% c("P01", "P06", "P18", "P21"))

cols(.default = col_character()) requests text columns instead of guessing. unique() shows distinct values, so "control" and "Control" can be noticed. %in% asks whether a value belongs to the listed set of IDs. A CSV importer may normally trim surrounding spaces; we temporarily keep them so we can see the problem rather than mistake automatic tidying for a clean source.
The file has 25 rows although the study has 24 plants. Confirm the duplicated ID:

raw |> count(plant_id) |> filter(n > 1)

count() counts rows by the named column. Repeated IDs can be legitimate if a table has one row per time point. Here the protocol says one row per plant, so we inspect both P01 rows and the source record before deciding what to do.

title: Day 11 — Check the table before trusting the answer
section: Make evidence-based repairs
text:
Make evidence-based repairs
The supplied field notes establish the following:

The two P01 rows are an accidental duplicate of the same record.
Control means control, and a trailing space on a treatment is accidental.
P18’s initial length is 18.7 mm; its cell includes the unit as text.
P21’s source record gives final length 43.8 mm, not the entered 4.38.
P06’s final measurement is unavailable. There is no supported replacement.

The number 4.38 alone would not justify multiplying by ten. The source record authorises that correction. Similarly, missing P06 is not a length of zero.

cleaned <- raw |>
  mutate(treatment = tolower(trimws(treatment)),
         initial_mm = if_else(plant_id == "P18", "18.7", initial_mm),
         final_mm = if_else(plant_id == "P21", "43.8", final_mm)) |>
  distinct() |>
  mutate(initial_mm = parse_double(initial_mm),
         final_mm = parse_double(final_mm),
         growth_mm = final_mm - initial_mm)

trimws() removes surrounding whitespace, and tolower() standardises letters in these documented labels. if_else(condition, yes, no) makes the stated replacement only for the identified record. distinct() removes exact repeated rows; we use it only after confirming the import duplication. parse_double() turns verified number text into numeric values, preserving missing values. These are worked repair instructions, not functions to memorise today.

title: Day 11 — Check the table before trusting the answer
section: Check the repaired table
text:
Check the repaired table

nrow(cleaned)
anyDuplicated(cleaned$plant_id)
sum(is.na(cleaned$growth_mm))
cleaned |> count(treatment)
write_csv(cleaned, "output/seedlings-cleaned.csv")

Expect 24 rows, zero duplicated IDs, and one missing growth value. Both groups still contain 12 plants, but the control group has only 11 observed growth values. Counting enrolled plants and counting usable measurements answer different questions. Keep the raw file, repair script, and field notes so another person can trace these decisions.

title: Day 11 — Check the table before trusting the answer
section: Your practical
text:
Your practical

Run the inspection steps before the repair block. Write comments recording what prompted each check.
Run the repairs and verify the expected counts. Inspect P06, P18, and P21.
Calculate the mean of cleaned$growth_mm with and without na.rm = TRUE. Explain what each result means; do not replace the missing value.
Save a short output/cleaning-notes.txt explaining the evidence for each change and the observation left unavailable.
Restart R, rerun your script, and confirm the original CSV has 25 rows while the derived CSV has 24. Different row counts are expected and documented.







Hint: avoid silently losing records





Inspect raw |> filter(plant_id == "P01") before using distinct(). Do not use distinct(plant_id, .keep_all = TRUE) to discard different records merely because they share an ID. Real disagreements need investigation.

title: Day 11 — Check the table before trusting the answer
section: Check your understanding
text:
Check your understanding






What makes a repair justified?





A check identifies a question; the source record supports the repair. A very small or large value may be real. Omitting missing values from a calculation does not make their absence disappear from the report.



Keep: day11-cleaning.R, the derived CSV, and your cleaning notes. Next: describe variation.

title: Day 10 — A first biological report
section: Today’s question
text:
Today’s question
What can we say about seedling growth from the measurements alone? Today is practice in carrying an analysis from saved data to a readable result. No new statistical test is required. The purpose is to combine skills you have already used and notice where you still need a reference or help.
Open your course project and save a copy of report.Rmd as first-report.Rmd in the project root. Keeping both source files there preserves the familiar data/ paths. Your generated HTML can go into reports/.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 10 — A first biological report
section: What a reader needs
text:
What a reader needs
A reader who was not in the room needs to know the question, what was measured, how you calculated the result, and what the figure shows. A list of function calls is not a methods explanation. “We calculated change in length as final minus initial length for each plant” explains the calculation in biological terms. The code makes the calculation repeatable.
The supplied experiment has 24 independently potted seedlings, twelve randomly assigned to each group. Initial and final measurements come from the same plant, seven days apart. The treatment label treated denotes a nutrient treatment; the nutrient formulation is unspecified. Do not invent details beyond the dictionary. These are simulated measurements.
Start with the familiar analysis:

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
seedlings <- read_csv("data/seedlings.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
seedlings <- mutate(seedlings, growth_mm = final_mm - initial_mm)

Put these lines in a code chunk before any result that depends on them. Give the reader a few simple checks:

nrow(seedlings)
sum(is.na(seedlings$growth_mm))
range(seedlings$growth_mm)

The file has 24 plants and no missing growth values. The minimum and maximum are measurements, not plausible bounds for every seedling in nature. The range summarises this dataset; it is sensitive to unusual observations.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 10 — A first biological report
section: A figure worth discussing
text:
A figure worth discussing
Recreate the plot of growth against treatment from day 8. Show every plant, label the growth axis in mm, and explain that each dot represents one independently potted plant. Include the caption and discuss the visible overlap between groups.
A useful opening could be: “Growth varied among individual plants in both groups.” Follow it with something specific you can see. Avoid declaring that a treatment “works” on the strength of a higher-looking cloud of points. We have not yet considered how much uncertainty surrounds a group comparison.
You can compute a simple mean for all plants using mean(seedlings$growth_mm). Make clear that this combines treatments and does not answer whether they differ. We will calculate and interpret group summaries during week 3.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 10 — A first biological report
section: Your practical: four short sections
text:
Your practical: four short sections
Create these sections in first-report.Rmd:

Question and data: state the question, the number of plants, the treatment allocation, and that these are simulated data. Explain the meaning of a row.
Methods: explain how the file was imported and how growth was derived. Include working code with relative paths. Say what the units are.
Results: include the labelled individual-plant figure and a small number of calculated facts that help answer the question. Use inline R for at least one result if you are comfortable; correct prose is more important than novelty.
Interpretation: write three or four sentences describing the pattern, variation, and an important limitation. No p-value is needed.

Now restart R and run this in the R Console, not inside the report (a report must not try to render itself):

rmarkdown::render("first-report.Rmd", output_dir = "reports")

If it fails, work from the first error. Do not repeatedly run random Console commands until it happens to work. Add missing prerequisites to the report.

title: Day 10 — A first biological report
section: Transfer to a second table
text:
Transfer to a second table
With remaining practice time, inspect data/leaf-mass.csv. It records one leaf from each of 18 independent plants, with area in square centimetres and dry mass in milligrams. Make an area-versus-mass scatter plot in a script called leaf-first-look.R. Use the actual column names from names(leaves) and do not subtract quantities with different units. A larger mass and a larger area may be associated; one does not establish that one causes the other.






Hint: adapting the plot





Start with leaves <- read_csv("data/leaf-mass.csv", show_col_types = FALSE). Then map leaf_area_cm2 to x and dry_mass_mg to y. The same plotting structure can serve a different question when you deliberately change the table, columns, labels, and explanation.

title: Day 10 — A first biological report
section: Completion check
text:
Completion check
Ask a partner to open the HTML without RStudio. Can they identify the question, units, meaning of a dot, and the main limitation? Then check your own source: can it render after restarting R? These checks concern readability and reproducibility, not marks.






Self-check





The .Rmd should contain the imports, derived column, and plot. The HTML should contain sentences that make sense without reading every code line. A personal path such as a username-specific Desktop location makes the report less portable.

title: Day 8 — Turn measurements into a useful figure
section: Today’s question
text:
Today’s question
Do plants that started longer also end longer? And how much did each plant grow? A new column and a labelled figure can answer these questions without editing cells by hand. Start a script called day08.R in your project root.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 8 — Turn measurements into a useful figure
section: Create a derived measurement
text:
Create a derived measurement

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
seedlings <- read_csv("data/seedlings.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
seedlings <- mutate(seedlings, growth_mm = final_mm - initial_mm)
head(seedlings)

mutate() returns a table with a new or changed column. We assign that returned table to seedlings. Within this function, R looks for final_mm and initial_mm in the supplied table. The original file on disk is unchanged. For P01, check 44.3 minus 25.7: the growth is 18.6 mm. A negative change would mean the recorded final length was smaller; it would deserve checking, not automatic deletion.
The new variable describes change, while final_mm describes size. These answer different questions. Always say which you are comparing.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 8 — Turn measurements into a useful figure
section: Select observations and variables
text:
Select observations and variables

control_plants <- filter(seedlings, treatment == "control")
growth_table <- select(seedlings, plant_id, treatment, growth_mm)

filter() selects rows satisfying a condition. == asks whether values are equal; it does not assign values. Quotation marks mark the text label "control". select() chooses columns. Neither operation changes the original raw CSV. Inspect control_plants: it should have twelve rows. growth_table should have 24 rows and three columns.
Sometimes it is easier to read a sequence from left to right:

longer_control <- seedlings |>
  filter(treatment == "control") |>
  filter(growth_mm > 15)

The base R pipe |> passes the result on its left as the first argument to the next function. Read this as “take seedlings, keep controls, then keep growth over 15 mm”. This is a convenience for joining steps, not a new biological operation. Run intermediate steps when diagnosing a problem.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 8 — Turn measurements into a useful figure
section: Map columns to a figure
text:
Map columns to a figure

size_plot <- ggplot(seedlings, aes(x = initial_mm, y = final_mm,
                                  colour = treatment)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  labs(x = "Initial seedling length (mm)",
       y = "Final seedling length (mm)",
       colour = "Treatment") +
  theme_minimal()
size_plot

ggplot() identifies the table. aes() maps columns to positions and colour. Each point is one plant. The + adds a layer or a display instruction to the figure. The plus at the end of a line tells R that the expression continues. Colour maps a group label; it does not mean the treatment is a numeric measurement.
Read the labels before interpreting the pattern. The horizontal axis is initial length, so this figure does not directly show growth. It also cannot by itself prove that starting longer causes a larger final length.

growth_plot <- ggplot(seedlings, aes(x = treatment, y = growth_mm)) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = 0.08, height = 0, seed = 8),
             alpha = 0.8) +
  labs(x = "Treatment", y = "Change in seedling length (mm)") +
  theme_minimal()
growth_plot

This shows growth for each group. A small horizontal jitter separates points that would overlap; height = 0 leaves every measured vertical value unchanged. seed = 8 makes this display repeatable. No test is needed today: describe what you can see, including overlap and variation among plants.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 8 — Turn measurements into a useful figure
section: Save something another application can read
text:
Save something another application can read



The worked figure shows individual seedling growth measurements by treatment; the groups overlap.



ggsave("output/seedling-growth.png", plot = growth_plot,
       width = 6, height = 4, dpi = 150)
write_csv(growth_table, "output/seedling-growth.csv")

The supplied project includes output/. These commands create files there; they may replace files with the same names. The plot object in memory and the PNG on disk are different things. Locate and open both saved outputs in the file manager.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 8 — Turn measurements into a useful figure
section: Your practical
text:
Your practical

Recreate both plots from the start of the script and calculate P02’s growth by hand to check the subtraction.
Save a table containing only treated plants’ IDs and growth measurements.
Choose one transfer task: make a plot of initial length against growth with axes labelled in mm, or adapt the same workflow to the organic-product table below. Do one, not both.
Write two sentences: one describing a visible pattern, one identifying a question the plot alone cannot settle.
Restart R and run the script. Confirm the saved files still open afterwards.


Alternative transfer task: a derived yield column
Our simulated table data/organic-recovery.csv records twelve separate runs of an organic synthesis, six assigned to each of two protocols, standard and modified. A run is one independently performed preparation. These labels identify procedures; you do not need to know their chemical steps.
Each row supplies a theoretical_mass_g: the maximum product mass from that run’s starting materials. isolated_mass_g is collected dry product, assumed pure for this simplified exercise. Both are grams. Calculate yield_percent = 100 × isolated_mass_g / theoretical_mass_g. You are given the maximum and do not need to derive it from a reaction. The first run, Y01, has 1.00 g maximum and 0.62 g collected, so its yield is 62%.

organic <- read_csv("data/organic-recovery.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
organic <- mutate(organic,
                  yield_percent = 100 * isolated_mass_g / theoretical_mass_g)
head(organic)

The runs started at different scales, so larger collected mass alone need not mean a greater yield. Inspect the supplied dictionary in data/README.md. Make a plot with protocol on x and percentage yield on y, using the familiar individual-point pattern. Label its y-axis “Isolated product yield (%)”. Save the derived table to output/organic-yields.csv and your plot to output/organic-yields.png. Keep its import and calculation in day08.R.






Hint: adapt the roles, not just the title





Use organic as the plot’s data, protocol for x, and yield_percent for y. Choose horizontal jitter with zero vertical jitter as above. Use write_csv() for the derived table and ggsave() for the figure. Expect 12 rows, no missing masses, and Y01 at 62%. A plot shows these results; it does not establish that one protocol is generally better or that a higher yield means purer product.









Hint: a plot or file is missing





Printing growth_plot shows the plot; assigning it alone may not. Check getwd() and dir.exists("output") if saving fails. If a column is not found, check names(seedlings) and run the earlier mutate() line.

title: Day 8 — Turn measurements into a useful figure
section: Check your understanding
text:
Check your understanding






Why keep the raw table?





A derived table lets someone trace the calculation back to the recorded lengths. P02 grew 8.0 mm. Selecting columns is not selecting plants; select() and filter() act on different parts of the table.



Keep: day08.R, your derived tables, and figures in output/. If you chose the organic transfer, its two organic-yields outputs replace the extra initial-length-versus-growth figure; retain the main seedling work. Next: put explanation and code in one report.

title: Day 6 — Let R keep track of a calculation
section: Today’s question
text:
Today’s question
A seedling was 20 mm long at the start of an experiment and 37 mm long at the end. How much did it grow? The answer is simple; our task is to make the computer keep a readable, repeatable record of how we obtained it. All plant measurements in this course are simulated teaching data, not results from a real experiment.
Open the extracted introcomputing-course folder and double-click introcomputing.Rproj. R is the program that calculates. RStudio is the workspace we use to write instructions, run R, inspect results, and prepare reports. Its Console accepts R instructions. An R script is a saved text file containing instructions. The terminal from week 1 accepts shell commands; do not type ls into the R Console or R expressions into the Ubuntu shell.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 6 — Let R keep track of a calculation
section: Start with a calculation
text:
Start with a calculation
Type the following in the R Console, pressing Enter after each line. Do not type the Console’s > prompt. The [1] in an answer labels the first printed element; it is not part of your measurement.

37 - 20
20 * 2
37 / 20

You should obtain 17, 40, and 1.85. The last value is a ratio, not a change in mm. The calculation can be correct while answering the wrong biological question.
Now choose File → New File → R Script, save it as day06.R in the project folder, and put this in the script:

# Measurements are lengths in millimetres.
initial_mm <- 20
final_mm <- 37
growth_mm <- final_mm - initial_mm
growth_mm

<- assigns the result on its right to a named object on its left. Read it as “store this value under this name”. A line beginning with # is a comment for people. R ignores the comment. To run a line from the editor, place the cursor on it and use Run. Saving a script does not run it; running a script does not save changes in the editor.
If RStudio is not ready, use the R and RStudio setup page. Keep the R reference sheet open while practising.
Object names are case-sensitive. growth_mm and Growth_mm are different names. An object in the Environment pane is in this R session’s memory. The script is a file on storage. Reopening the script does not recreate the object until you run the instructions.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 6 — Let R keep track of a calculation
section: One name can hold several values
text:
One name can hold several values
c() combines values into a vector, an ordered collection. Functions have names followed by parentheses; the values inside are their arguments.

initial_mm <- c(20, 22, 19)
final_mm <- c(37, 40, 34)
growth_mm <- final_mm - initial_mm
growth_mm
mean(growth_mm)
length(growth_mm)

The growth values are 17, 18, and 15 mm. R subtracts position by position here. mean() calculates their average, approximately 16.67 mm. length() counts values and gives 3. This only makes biological sense because both vectors list the same three plants in the same order. Matching observations matters.
Numbers, text, and logical values are different kinds of data:

plant_id <- c("P01", "P02", "P03")
growth_mm > 16

The comparison gives TRUE TRUE FALSE. Quotation marks identify text; "20" is text whereas 20 is a number. Plant IDs belong in text even if they contain numbers. To open help for a function, run ?mean in the Console and read its Description and Examples rather than every option.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 6 — Let R keep track of a calculation
section: Your practical
text:
Your practical

Keep the three-plant calculation in day06.R and explain the units in comments.
Add a fourth plant that grew from 21 to 39 mm. Extend both vectors, rerun the calculation, and check length(growth_mm).
Choose one ratio exercise: calculate each plant’s final/initial ratio in an object called length_ratio, explaining how it differs from growth in mm; or use the product-yield calculation below. Both practise division and named inputs; you do not need to do both.
Change the first final length from 37 to 38 mm. Predict which growth value changes and check your prediction.
Save the script, restart R through Session → Restart R, and run its lines from the top. Everything it needs should be in the script.


Alternative ratio exercise: how much product was collected?
In a synthesis, starting materials are used to make a product. For this simulated example, the maximum possible product mass has already been calculated for you: 1.00 g. Call it theoretical_mass_g. The collected dry product has mass 0.62 g, called isolated_mass_g. Assume this collected material is pure product for this simplified calculation. You do not need a reaction equation.
Percentage yield means the collected product as a percentage of the supplied maximum. Compute 100 × isolated mass / theoretical mass, using the same mass unit for both. Put this calculation in day06.R if you chose this alternative:

theoretical_mass_g <- 1.00
isolated_mass_g <- 0.62
yield_percent <- 100 * isolated_mass_g / theoretical_mass_g
yield_percent

The answer is 62%. The gram units cancel in the ratio. Predict the result if collected mass changes to 0.70 g, then rerun; it should be 70%. Add a comment explaining why 0.62 g is a mass and 62% is a proportion relative to a maximum. A larger percentage does not establish greater purity or safety. This is numerical practice, not instructions for carrying out a chemical experiment.






Hint: an object is not found





Check the spelling, including capitals, and run the line that creates the object. An editor line has no effect until it runs. If the Console shows +, an expression is unfinished: check quotes or parentheses, or press Esc to cancel it.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 6 — Let R keep track of a calculation
section: Check your understanding
text:
Check your understanding

What survives restarting R: an unsaved object or a saved script?
Why is mean(plant_id) not a useful operation?
What must be true for two vectors to be subtracted position by position?







Check your answers





The saved script survives; objects must be recreated. IDs name plants rather than measure quantities, so an average ID has no meaning. The vectors must refer to corresponding observations in the same order and have compatible lengths.



Keep: day06.R, with the four-plant example and comments about units. Next: import a whole table.
