text: Lecture slides · Weekly self-check

title: Day 5 — Share laboratory files, then meet R
section: Repeat a useful workflow
text:
Repeat a useful workflow
Today you will repeat yesterday’s investigation with fewer prompts. Repetition helps make file handling a tool you can rely on. The biological task remains: identify the treated samples and prepare a small package that another person can understand.
We then meet R, which will calculate and plot the measurements. The terminal and R console are different places to enter instructions; recognising the difference will prevent a common beginner problem.

title: Day 5 — Share laboratory files, then meet R
section: Practical 1: a fresh investigation folder
text:
Practical 1: a fresh investigation folder
Return to your shell workspace:
cd ~/introcomputing-shell
pwd
Use commands from the previous lessons to do the following. Read the whole list once before starting.

Create a fresh folder called day5.
Copy lab-data.zip into it and move into day5.
List the archive’s contents without extracting it.
Extract it into a folder called lab-data inside day5.
Enter the extracted folder and read the README.
Print the treated sample records and save them as treated-samples.txt.
Count the matching records using a pipe. Explain why the result is two.







Help me get started without doing everything





From the workspace use mkdir day5, cp lab-data.zip day5/, then cd day5. The slash after day5/ makes it clear that this destination is a directory. Use unzip -l lab-data.zip before unzip lab-data.zip -d lab-data. If a name already exists, inspect it before choosing whether to reuse it.









I cannot remember the search commands





Inside the extracted folder use grep -F treated samples.tsv. Add > treated-samples.txt to save the output, or | wc -l to count it. Do not redirect output into samples.tsv: that is the original input.

title: Day 5 — Share laboratory files, then meet R
section: Practical 2: make a package another person can inspect
text:
Practical 2: make a package another person can inspect
Inside the extracted lab-data folder, make a folder called report. Copy treated-samples.txt into it. Copy README.txt into it with the destination name context.txt. These copies keep the original files available.
Through the file manager, add report/findings.txt with four short statements: the number of samples, which received treatment, what the measurements mean, and what you have not yet analysed. For example, identifying a treated sample does not establish that its treatment changed growth.






Copy and rename commands





mkdir report
cp treated-samples.txt report/
cp README.txt report/context.txt
Create your own findings text in a plain-text editor. Check its saved location with ls report before packaging the folder.



Create and inspect a ZIP package:
zip -r report-bundle.zip report/
unzip -l report-bundle.zip
unzip report-bundle.zip -d review
ls review/report
zip creates an archive. -r includes the folder’s contents recursively, including any nested folders. unzip -l lets you inspect the package, then extraction into review tests what a recipient would receive. You should find context.txt, findings.txt, and treated-samples.txt inside review/report. Open findings.txt from there and check it is readable.
An archive is a snapshot of the files included when it was created or updated. Editing the ordinary report/findings.txt does not automatically update the ZIP. Make a new clearly named package after making changes. An archive stored only next to its originals is still vulnerable if the whole computer is lost.

title: Day 5 — Share laboratory files, then meet R
section: Practical 3: choose one transfer check
text:
Practical 3: choose one transfer check
Choose the partner explanation below or the organic-laboratory file task that follows. They practise the same file skills; you do not need to do both.

Explain the seedling files to a partner
Take turns. Point to the original archive, extracted source files, selected records, your findings, and the final report archive. Explain the role of each. Ask your partner to locate a particular measurement file using the manifest. Check the path rather than relying on a file that happened to be open already.
If the supported remote environment is ready, repeat just the navigation and inspection part there. Use the provided transfer route to move a small file, then identify the local and remote copies. If it is not ready, this step waits; the local practical still stands on its own.


Or: find records in a small organic-laboratory inventory
An inventory is a list of samples. Our simulated organic-chemistry inventory already labels each sample with a class, such as alcohol or ester. These are supplied text labels; you do not need to recognise a molecular structure or know its reactions. The task is simply to find the records labelled ester.

Download organic-lab.zip and locate it in your file manager. As on day 4, open ~/introcomputing-shell graphically and copy the download there. A browser download is not automatically in Ubuntu.
Return to that workspace in the shell, list the archive before extracting, then extract to a fresh organic-lab folder and enter it. Read README.txt and DICTIONARY.txt with less before inspecting inventory.tsv.
Use grep -F ester inventory.tsv to print matching records. Save them in ester-samples.txt and use a pipe to count them. Locate the saved extract in the file manager, then explain which file remained unchanged.







Hint: the same commands, different filenames





cd ~/introcomputing-shell
unzip -l organic-lab.zip
unzip organic-lab.zip -d organic-lab
cd organic-lab
less README.txt
less DICTIONARY.txt
head inventory.tsv
grep -F ester inventory.tsv > ester-samples.txt
grep -F ester inventory.tsv | wc -l
There are four sample records plus a header. Two records match: O02 and O03. The header does not contain ester. This command matches literal text, not chemical structures or a particular table column. The extracted organic-recovery.csv is for later calculations; you do not need to analyse it today. If the extraction folder already exists, inspect it and use a fresh name.

title: Day 5 — Share laboratory files, then meet R
section: Meet R and RStudio
text:
Meet R and RStudio
R is a language and computing environment for working with data. RStudio is an application that provides an editor, an R console, and other tools around R. The editor holds saved instructions; the console runs them. A terminal is a shell prompt, not an R console.
Open RStudio using the R/RStudio setup instructions. If it is not installed yet, watch the demonstration and use setup support before week 2. In the R console, enter:
44.3 - 25.7
R should return 18.6: the increase in length of plant P01, in millimetres. The console might print [1] before the answer. That marks the position of the first displayed element; it is not part of the measurement.
Enter this small supplied example in the R console:
initial_mm <- c(25.7, 24.3, 18.0)
final_mm <- c(44.3, 32.3, 32.9)
plot(initial_mm, final_mm,
     xlab = "Initial length (mm)",
     ylab = "Final length (mm)")
The c(...) pieces collect three values. <- gives each collection a name. plot(...) makes a scatter plot: each point is one plant with an initial and a final length. We will learn these ideas carefully next week; today identify the axes and check that there are three points. This example includes only three plants, not the full experiment.
Do not paste cd, grep, or unzip at the R prompt. Likewise, do not paste R calculations into the Ubuntu shell and expect R to run them automatically. When a command fails, first identify which program is reading it.

title: Day 5 — Share laboratory files, then meet R
section: From a plot to a report
text:
From a plot to a report
The teacher will show a complete HTML report generated from saved measurements and an R Markdown file. Notice the biological question, code, figure with units, and a written interpretation. The goal is to make these together so that the report can be produced again when new measurements arrive. You will build your first version next week.

title: Day 5 — Share laboratory files, then meet R
section: Check your understanding
text:
Check your understanding






Why inspect an archive after making it?





The name of the ZIP does not guarantee what it contains. Listing and extracting it checks the folder structure and the actual saved files a recipient gets.









Where should grep run, and where should 44.3 - 25.7 run?





Use grep in the terminal’s shell. Enter the calculation in the R console. The prompt tells you which program is waiting for instructions; learn to check it before entering a command.



Save today: a tested report-bundle.zip and the ordinary report folder. Add one sentence to findings.txt explaining how the package differs from its extracted contents. Repackage it if you want that change included in the ZIP. If you chose the inventory transfer check, also keep organic-lab/ester-samples.txt in the shell workspace.
Next: R objects, calculations, and vectors.

title: Day 3 — The terminal describes the same folders
text: Lecture slides · Weekly self-check

title: Day 3 — The terminal describes the same folders
section: Why type commands?
text:
Why type commands?
The terminal gives us another way to ask the computer to work with files. It becomes useful when we repeat a task, inspect many text records, or work on a remote computer. The folders have not become a new kind of object: we are describing the same locations using words instead of clicks.
Today we will create a small shell workspace and move between its folders. Tomorrow it will hold files from a biological laboratory exercise.

title: Day 3 — The terminal describes the same folders
section: Open the right terminal
text:
Open the right terminal
Follow the supported Windows/Mac setup page. Windows students use Ubuntu for these commands. Mac students use Terminal. If local installation is unavailable, the teacher will help arrange a supported environment. Do not spend the lesson trying to repair system settings alone.
On Windows, Ubuntu has a different home folder from Windows itself. For this week’s terminal exercises we deliberately use a separate folder in the Ubuntu home directory. Our native RStudio project will stay in the laptop Documents folder. We will practise transferring a file between these places explicitly.
A shell reads a command and starts the requested program. The terminal is the window through which we interact with the shell. You might see something like this:
anna@laptop:~$
This is a prompt. It means the shell is ready. Your prompt will differ and may end with % on a Mac. Do not type the prompt, $, or % from an example. Type the command and press Enter once to run it.

title: Day 3 — The terminal describes the same folders
section: Worked example: where am I?
text:
Worked example: where am I?
Run each line separately:
pwd
ls
pwd prints the current working directory. It might print /home/anna in Ubuntu or /Users/anna on a Mac. These are examples, not text to type. ls lists the names inside the current directory. Your list need not match anyone else’s.
Now create our workspace:
cd
mkdir -p introcomputing-shell/practice
cd introcomputing-shell
pwd
ls
cd means change directory; without a destination, it takes you home. mkdir means make directory. The option -p allows it to create the parent folder too and to accept folders that already exist. The final ls should include practice. An empty folder is still a real folder.

title: Day 3 — The terminal describes the same folders
section: Check it in the file manager
text:
Check it in the file manager
In Ubuntu on Windows, run:
explorer.exe .
In Mac Terminal, run:
open .
The dot means the current directory. The graphical window should show the practice folder. Leave this window open for the next exercise. On a remote Linux system these laptop-specific commands are not the remote file-transfer method; follow the supplied remote instructions instead.

title: Day 3 — The terminal describes the same folders
section: Practical 1: make a map and follow it
text:
Practical 1: make a map and follow it
From introcomputing-shell, run:
cd practice
mkdir seedlings
mkdir observations
ls
cd seedlings
pwd
cd ..
pwd
.. means the parent directory. The two pwd results should end in /practice/seedlings and /practice. Compare the file manager with this tree:
introcomputing-shell/
└── practice/
    ├── seedlings/
    └── observations/
Use the graphical window to open seedlings. Does this make the terminal move there too? Run pwd to check. Each window can have its own current location. Clicking in one does not automatically change the other.

title: Day 3 — The terminal describes the same folders
section: Commands, arguments, and options
text:
Commands, arguments, and options
In cd seedlings, cd is the command and seedlings is its argument: the destination. In ls -l, -l is an option asking for a longer listing. You do not need to interpret every column yet; identify which column contains names.
Try these from practice:
ls -l
cd observations
ls
An empty listing from ls means there are no visible entries to list. It does not mean the command failed. Many commands report success by simply returning to the prompt.

title: Day 3 — The terminal describes the same folders
section: Practical 2: recover from an ordinary mistake
text:
Practical 2: recover from an ordinary mistake
Return to practice with cd .., then try cd Observations. We created observations with a lowercase o. Ubuntu distinguishes uppercase and lowercase names. Many Macs do not distinguish them on their default disk, so this may work there. Always match the actual spelling so your work transfers between computers.
Now deliberately try:
cd no-such-folder
Read the message. The folder is missing; your computer has not broken. Run pwd and ls before trying again. Ask “where am I, and what is actually here?”






I’m lost. How can I return to the workspace?





Run cd ~/introcomputing-shell, then pwd. ~ is shorthand for your home directory. This route works even if you have navigated into several nested folders. Do not replace it with someone else’s username.

title: Day 3 — The terminal describes the same folders
section: Small keyboard habits that save effort
text:
Small keyboard habits that save effort

Tab: type the first few letters of a folder, then Tab to complete a name when it is unambiguous. Try cd pra then Tab from the workspace.
Up arrow: recall a previous command. Read it before running it again.
Ctrl+C: interrupt a running command or clear a partly typed command. This is different from copying selected text. Ubuntu terminal windows commonly use Ctrl+Shift+C/V for copying and pasting; Mac uses Command+C/V.
Quotes: keep a name containing spaces together, for example mkdir "field notes". Without quotes those words can become separate arguments.

We are not using deletion commands today. Practise on the supplied workspace, and ask before removing something you did not mean to create.

title: Day 3 — The terminal describes the same folders
section: Check your understanding
text:
Check your understanding






What changes when I run cd? What stays unchanged?





The terminal’s current working directory changes. The files do not move, and other windows need not change location. pwd checks the new starting point.









Why can ls work without printing any filenames?





The directory may be empty. Compare with an error, which normally includes a message explaining the problem. Read the output rather than assuming silence is failure.



Save today: the shell workspace and its folder tree. In a plain-text file called navigation-notes.txt inside that workspace, record the full path printed by pwd, your route back from home, and three commands with their meanings. Create the note through the graphical window if that is easiest.
Next: open an archive of laboratory files.

title: Day 1 — Find, save, and reopen your laboratory files
text: Lecture slides · Weekly self-check

title: Day 1 — Find, save, and reopen your laboratory files
section: Today’s biological question
text:
Today’s biological question
Did seedlings grow differently after a treatment? Before we calculate anything, we need to know which measurements belong to which plant and where those measurements are saved. A useful analysis starts with finding the right file.
Our measurements are simulated teaching data, not observations from an actual experiment. Imagine 24 seedlings, each in its own pot. Twelve pots received a treatment and twelve were controls. We measured each plant at the beginning and end. The treatment was assigned randomly. A control is a comparison group: it helps us judge what might have happened without the treatment.
Today you will download the course files, identify a table of measurements, and find your work again after closing every window. No programming is needed.

title: Day 1 — Find, save, and reopen your laboratory files
section: A file is different from the application that opens it
text:
A file is different from the application that opens it
A file is a saved collection of information with a name. A photograph, a table of measurements, and a written report can each be files. An application is a program that opens or changes files. The same table can be opened by several applications.
For example, seedlings.csv is a file. Excel, a text editor, and R can all read it. Closing Excel does not delete the saved file. Deleting the saved file is a different action. A file can also exist without any application displaying it.
A folder, also called a directory, groups files and other folders. Your computer’s file system organises these folders and records where files are stored. You can explore it using File Explorer on Windows or Finder on Mac. A browser such as Firefox or Safari displays websites; it is a different application from the file manager.

title: Day 1 — Find, save, and reopen your laboratory files
section: Practical 1: download and locate the course folder
text:
Practical 1: download and locate the course folder

Download the course files.
Open the browser’s downloads list. Use its option to show the download in File Explorer or Finder. Notice the folder’s name, usually Downloads.
Find course-files.zip. A ZIP archive is a package containing files and folders. On Windows, right-click it and choose Extract All. On Mac, double-click it to extract it. If the browser already extracted it, locate the resulting folder instead.
Find the extracted folder called introcomputing-course. Move this ordinary folder into Documents using the file manager. Do not work inside the ZIP’s preview window.
Open introcomputing-course. You should see a data folder, an output folder, a reports folder, report.Rmd, and introcomputing.Rproj.
Open data and find seedlings.csv. Keep this file unchanged.

Your computer may have a cloud-managed Documents folder. Tell the teacher if it does: we will check that your course files are actually available on the laptop, including when the network is disconnected. A shortcut or a cloud icon is not the same thing as a complete local copy.






I see two course folders. Which should I use?





Extraction can create an extra outer folder. Open folders until you find the one that directly contains data, output, and introcomputing.Rproj. That is the project folder. Move that whole folder together. Ask for help if filenames end in (1) because you downloaded several copies; choose one working copy rather than guessing between them later.

title: Day 1 — Find, save, and reopen your laboratory files
section: Reading names and extensions
text:
Reading names and extensions
The final part of a filename, such as .csv or .jpg, is its extension. It gives a clue about the format of the saved information. A CSV is a text table in which commas separate values. Changing the name seedlings.csv to seedlings.jpg would not turn measurements into a photograph.
Make extensions visible. In Windows File Explorer, look for View → Show → File name extensions; older versions place the checkbox directly under View. In Finder, use Settings → Advanced → Show all filename extensions. Menu wording can vary. Ask for help if you cannot find the setting.

title: Day 1 — Find, save, and reopen your laboratory files
section: Practical 2: open a copy in two ways
text:
Practical 2: open a copy in two ways

Copy data/seedlings.csv and paste the copy into output.
Rename the copy seedlings-practice.csv. Confirm that it still ends in .csv.
Open this practice copy. If a spreadsheet opens automatically, notice its rows and columns, then close it without saving changes.
Right-click the practice file and choose Open with a text editor, such as Notepad on Windows or TextEdit on Mac. Do not save changes here either.

The first lines should contain the following information:
plant_id,treatment,initial_mm,final_mm
P01,control,25.7,44.3
P02,control,24.3,32.3
The first line is a header naming the columns. The next line describes plant P01. Its initial length was 25.7 millimetres and its final length was 44.3 millimetres. A spreadsheet displays the commas as column boundaries; the text editor displays the commas themselves. Both applications opened the same file.
Discuss: did P01 grow by 44.3 mm, or did it end at 44.3 mm? Its increase was 44.3 − 25.7 = 18.6 mm. Keeping the meaning and units of a measurement matters as much as knowing how to open its file.

title: Day 1 — Find, save, and reopen your laboratory files
section: Practical 3: save a note you can find again
text:
Practical 3: save a note you can find again
Open a plain-text editor and write three short sentences: what a row represents, what the length units are, and where the original measurements are stored. Use Save As and save the note as day01-notes.txt in reports.
On Mac, choose Format → Make Plain Text in TextEdit before saving. On either system, check the resulting filename in the file manager. It should not secretly end in .txt.txt or .rtf.
Close the editor and all file-manager windows. Open the file manager again and navigate from Documents to your note. Open it. If you can only find it through an application’s “recent files” list, repeat the folder route once more.

title: Day 1 — Find, save, and reopen your laboratory files
section: Check your understanding
text:
Check your understanding
Try answering before opening the explanation.






Does closing an application delete the file? What did copying create?





Closing an application does not delete a saved file. Copying created another file. Changes to your practice copy would not automatically change the original. Neither copy is protected against losing the computer if both are stored only on that computer.









Why keep data/seedlings.csv unchanged?





It is our starting record. Later we will describe changes in code so that someone else can repeat the analysis and see what happened to the original measurements.



Save today: reports/day01-notes.txt and output/seedlings-practice.csv. Be ready to show their locations without relying on “recent files”.
Next: folders, paths, and what a computer does.

title: Statistics reference: describe, compare, and interpret
text:
Start with the biological question and the independent experimental unit. Neither a large table nor a small p-value can repair a design with no independent replication.
An interval around the mean does not describe where 95% of individual plants will fall. Adding technical repeats of the same plant does not add independent plants to the sample size.

title: Statistics reference: describe, compare, and interpret
section: The two comparisons taught here
text:
The two comparisons taught here
Independent groups: separate plants/pots allocated to control and treatment. Use a guided Welch two-sample t-test for the difference in mean growth. Define the direction before reporting it, such as treated minus control.
Paired observations: the same plant before and after a change. Compute after minus before within each plant, then analyse the differences. Correctly matching identifiers is essential; row order in two files is not evidence of matching pairs.
Both approaches need independent experimental units or pairs. For small samples, inspect unusual observations and strong skew. A test is conditional on its assumptions; you are not learning an automatic test-selection algorithm.
A p-value is the probability, under the null model and its assumptions, of a test statistic at least as extreme as the observed one. It is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true. Report the estimated difference, its units, confidence interval, sample sizes, and a biological interpretation. A small p-value does not establish a large or causal effect; a large one does not establish equality.

title: Statistics reference: describe, compare, and interpret
section: A straight line
text:
A straight line
In lm(y ~ x, data = table), the intercept is fitted y at x = 0 and the slope is the fitted change in y for a one-unit increase in x. The slope’s units are y-units per x-unit. The residual is observed y minus fitted y.
For calibration, standards have known x values; invert the fitted line to obtain an unknown concentration from its signal, only within a supported range. This simple calculation provides a point estimate, without full uncertainty propagation. For an observational biological association, the slope does not establish what would happen if we intervened to change x.
See week 3 and week 4 for worked examples.

title: Glossary: words we use in this course
text:
Word
Meaning here




File
A named, saved collection of information, such as text, measurements, or a picture


Folder / directory
A container organising files and other folders


File system
The way an operating system stores and organises files and directories


Path
An address locating a file or directory on a particular computer


Extension
A filename ending such as .csv, .R, .Rmd, or .html, indicating its intended format


Home directory
The starting personal folder for an account on a computer


Working directory
The folder relative paths currently start from


Operating system
Software managing the computer and the applications running on it


CPU
The processor that carries out instructions


RAM / memory
Working storage used by running programs; save work to persistent files


Process
A running instance of a program


Bit / byte
A bit is 0 or 1; a byte contains eight bits, with 256 possible patterns


Terminal
A window or interface through which you interact with a shell


Shell
A program interpreting commands such as cd and ls


Console
In this course, usually the R interface that reads R expressions


Local / remote
On your current laptop / on another computer reached over a network


SSH
A secure connection to a remote shell


Remote desktop
A graphical session on a remote computer


Archive
A package containing files and folders, for example a ZIP


CSV / TSV
Text tables whose fields are separated by commas / tabs


Object
A named value held in an R session


Function
A named operation applied to inputs, such as mean()


Argument
An input or setting given to a function or command


Package
A collection of R functions and related resources


Observation
A recorded measurement or set of measurements; not necessarily an independent replicate


Experimental unit
The independently allocated entity, such as a pot or culture flask


Technical replicate
A repeated measurement of the same underlying sample


Missing value
A measurement that is unavailable; represented by NA in R


Raw data
The original supplied measurements, preserved without overwriting


Theoretical mass
In the organic practice, the supplied maximum possible product mass for a run


Isolated mass
In the organic practice, the dry product collected, assumed pure for the simplified calculation


Percentage yield
100 × isolated mass / theoretical mass, using the same mass units


Percentage point
A difference on a percentage scale: 70% minus 60% is 10 percentage points


Derived data
Values calculated or cleaned from the originals with documented code


Render / Knit
Run a report’s code and combine results with its text to create a document


Reproducibility
Being able to regenerate a result from its stated inputs, code, and environment

title: Windows: install Ubuntu; Mac: open Terminal
text:
We will use a terminal to give the computer short written instructions. On Windows we use Ubuntu, a version of Linux, through Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL). Mac users can use the Terminal application already on their Mac.
You do not need to understand the commands yet. This page gets you ready for the first exercises. Installation help will be provided during the course.

title: Windows: install Ubuntu; Mac: open Terminal
section: Windows: install Ubuntu
text:
Windows: install Ubuntu

1. Prepare
Save your work: installation may require restarting your computer. You need an internet connection and permission to install software. On a university-managed computer, ask the teaching team if administrator access is unavailable.
Use Windows 11 for this setup. Microsoft’s installation command also supports Windows 10 version 2004 (build 19041) or later; if you have an older system, ask for help choosing a supported course environment.


2. Open PowerShell as administrator
Open Start, type PowerShell, right-click Windows PowerShell, and choose Run as administrator. Accept the Windows permission prompt.
PowerShell is a Windows command window. We use it for installation; later Linux exercises belong in Ubuntu.


3. Install
In PowerShell, type this command and press Enter:
wsl --install -d Ubuntu
Wait for it to finish and restart the computer if requested. This installs Ubuntu alongside your Windows applications using WSL.
These steps follow Microsoft’s WSL installation instructions.


4. Open Ubuntu and create your Linux account
After restarting, open Start, search for Ubuntu, and open it. First startup may take a little time.
When asked, choose a Linux username, for example anna, using lowercase letters. Then choose a password and enter it again when prompted. This is a separate account from your Windows account.
Nothing appears while you type the password, not even dots. This is normal. Type it and press Enter. Keep the password somewhere secure; do not send it to a teacher or include it in a screenshot.
When setup finishes, you should see a line ending in a prompt, often $. The prompt means Ubuntu is waiting for a command. Do not type the $ itself.
The account and password behaviour is described in Microsoft’s environment setup guide.


5. Check Ubuntu
In Ubuntu, run these commands one at a time:
whoami
pwd
uname -s
whoami should show your Linux username. pwd shows your current folder, usually /home/ followed by your username. uname -s should print Linux.
To check WSL itself, open PowerShell and run:
wsl --list --verbose
Look for an Ubuntu entry with 2 in the VERSION column. A running or stopped state is normal. If your installation shows version 1, bring it to the setup session so we can help check it.


6. Opening Ubuntu next time
Open Ubuntu from Start. You normally do not need administrator mode for course exercises. Closing its window does not delete your saved files.

title: Windows: install Ubuntu; Mac: open Terminal
section: Mac: use Terminal directly
text:
Mac: use Terminal directly
Open Finder, then Applications → Utilities → Terminal. You can also search for Terminal with Spotlight. You do not need to install Ubuntu.
Run the same three commands:
whoami
pwd
uname -s
Your home folder is usually /Users/ followed by your username, and uname -s prints Darwin, the underlying macOS system. That is expected. macOS is not Linux, but the basic commands we use work in both environments. A prompt ending in % is also normal on a Mac.
Commands labelled Ubuntu only, such as apt, do not belong in Mac Terminal.

title: Windows: install Ubuntu; Mac: open Terminal
section: First exercise: a folder you can find again
text:
First exercise: a folder you can find again
On Windows use Ubuntu; on Mac use Terminal. Run one line at a time:
cd
mkdir -p introcomputing/first-session
cd introcomputing/first-session
pwd
ls

cd on its own takes you to your home folder.
mkdir -p creates the named folders if they do not already exist.
cd introcomputing/first-session moves into that folder.
pwd prints its full location, called its path.
ls lists what is inside. A new, empty folder produces no listed filenames.

Now see the same folder in a graphical file manager:
Windows — run in Ubuntu:
explorer.exe .
Mac — run in Terminal:
open .
The dot means “the folder I am in now”. The file-manager window and the terminal are showing the same place in two different ways.
Close the terminal, reopen it, and find your folder again:
cd ~/introcomputing/first-session
pwd
Here ~ is shorthand for your home folder. Being able to return to saved work is part of being ready, even when the folder is still empty.

title: Windows: install Ubuntu; Mac: open Terminal
section: Windows and Ubuntu have different home folders
text:
Windows and Ubuntu have different home folders
On Windows, Ubuntu’s /home/anna is different from Windows’ C:\Users\anna. A file downloaded by your Windows browser does not automatically appear in your Ubuntu home folder. For terminal exercises, use the Ubuntu home folder we just created. We will practise locating downloads and transferring files together.
You can reach Ubuntu files through explorer.exe ., or by entering \\wsl$ in File Explorer’s address bar and opening your Ubuntu distribution. See Microsoft’s guide to Windows and Linux file systems.
R and RStudio will have separate setup instructions. You do not need to install them inside Ubuntu to complete this page.

title: Install R and RStudio; open your course project
text:
R performs calculations. RStudio is the application in which we write code, inspect results, and make reports. Install both on your laptop, or use the supported remote applications when access details are provided.
These steps are for native Windows or macOS applications. Windows students do not need to install a second copy of R inside Ubuntu/WSL. The Linux command-line setup is a separate page.

title: Install R and RStudio; open your course project
section: 1. Install R
text:
1. Install R
Go to CRAN’s R downloads and choose your operating system. On Windows choose the base installation, then the standard installer. On Mac choose the installer matching your Mac’s processor and supported macOS version; About This Mac identifies the processor. If the choices are unclear, bring your computer to the setup session. Install R before RStudio.
R is available for Windows, macOS, and Linux through the R Project and CRAN.

title: Install R and RStudio; open your course project
section: 2. Install RStudio Desktop
text:
2. Install RStudio Desktop
Download the free RStudio Desktop installer from Posit. Choose your operating system, install it, then open RStudio. You do not need to purchase a product or create a cloud account. Check the download page’s current system requirements if your computer is older. RStudio requires an R installation, as explained in Posit’s download guide.
Find the Console pane. Its prompt is usually >. Type:
2 + 3
Press Enter. The result should be [1] 5. The [1] labels the first element printed; it is not part of your answer or something you type.

title: Install R and RStudio; open your course project
section: 3. Install the small package set
text:
3. Install the small package set
Packages add functions to R. In the R console, run this once while connected to the internet:
install.packages(c("readr", "dplyr", "ggplot2", "rmarkdown", "knitr"))
Wait until the prompt returns. Keep installation commands out of your analysis and report: they change the computer’s setup and need not run every time. Load packages in each new analysis session using library().
If asked to compile packages from source on Windows or Mac, ask for help using the available binary packages. Installing compilers is not a course exercise.

title: Install R and RStudio; open your course project
section: 4. Download and extract the course folder
text:
4. Download and extract the course folder
If you extracted the course folder during day 1, reuse that same folder and continue with step 4 below. Do not make a second project just for this setup check.

If you do not already have it, download course-files.zip.
Find it in your browser’s downloads, then show it in the file manager.
On Windows, right-click and choose Extract All; on Mac, double-click the ZIP. Move the extracted introcomputing-course folder to a place you can find again, such as Documents. Extract the whole folder, not a single file.
Inside the extracted folder, open introcomputing.Rproj in RStudio. A ZIP preview in Windows is not an extracted project.

Your folder should look like this:
introcomputing-course/
├── introcomputing.Rproj
├── report.Rmd
├── START-HERE.txt
├── data/
│   ├── README.md
│   ├── seedlings.csv
│   └── ...
├── output/
└── reports/
The .Rproj file tells RStudio which folder is this project. Data remain ordinary files inside it. In the R console run:
getwd()
file.exists("data/seedlings.csv")
The first result should end with introcomputing-course; the second should be TRUE. data/seedlings.csv means “inside the data folder of this project”. Do not replace it with a path containing your own username.

title: Install R and RStudio; open your course project
section: 5. Check packages and the first report
text:
5. Check packages and the first report
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
packageVersion("rmarkdown")
If these commands finish without an error, open report.Rmd from RStudio’s Files pane and click Knit. A report with a table and a growth plot should appear. Its data are simulated. You will learn to explain and modify this report in week 2; you are checking the installation now.
R Markdown uses Pandoc to make the output document; RStudio supplies it. You do not need a PDF/LaTeX installation for our HTML reports. R Markdown’s installation documentation describes these dependencies.

section: If something goes wrong
text:
If something goes wrong







Symptom
First check




RStudio cannot find R
Check that R installed successfully before RStudio.


“There is no package called …”
Run the package installation line in the R console, then load the package again.


file.exists() is FALSE
Open the extracted .Rproj; look for an extra nested folder after extraction.


The console shows + instead of >
An expression is unfinished. Press Esc and check closing quotes or brackets.


Knit reports “object not found”
The report needs code creating the object; an object made only in the console is insufficient.


An installation or permissions error persists
Save the exact error and use the setup session; the remote route is an alternative once available.

title: Data Analysis in Life Sciences
text:
Learn how computers organise information, how to work in a Linux command line, and how to use R to turn biological measurements into figures and reproducible reports.
We start with files and folders. You do not need previous programming experience. Each lesson combines an explanation, a worked example, and a practical where you save something you can find and use again. The biology includes seedling growth, photosynthesis, calibration measurements, and a small duckweed experiment. Short transfer choices also use basic organic-laboratory records, such as the percentage of a supplied maximum product mass collected. Each exercise explains the required quantities and calculation; prior chemistry is not required.

Getting started

Windows: install Ubuntu; Mac: open Terminal.

Download the course project and laboratory archive.
Working on a remote Linux computer.

title: What you will learn and how to work
text: Data Analysis in Life Sciences is a five-week introduction to computing and biological data analysis. We start with finding a file and end with an analysis that another person can reproduce. The workflow is meant to carry into later biology practicals, where R replaces manual spreadsheet calculations and graph preparation.

title: What you will learn and how to work
section: What you should become able to do
text:
What you should become able to do

Explain files, folders, paths, applications, memory, storage, and processes through the practical actions you use every day.
Organise and inspect lab files with a small set of command-line tools.
Connect to a supplied remote Linux environment and distinguish its files from the files on your laptop.
Import and check biological measurements in R, calculate derived variables, summarise groups, and make labelled plots.
Interpret mean, variance, SD, and the difference between individual spread and uncertainty in an estimate.
Interpret a guided t-test and a straight-line fit, with attention to independent experimental units, units of measurement, and limitations.
Write and render an R Markdown report from its saved data and code.

No previous file-system, terminal, R, or statistics knowledge is assumed. We will practise the same actions several times, with gradually less guidance. Later courses will develop biological theory and bioinformatics tools; this course does not teach database searching, sequence alignment, or omics analysis.
Prior chemistry courses are not required to understand an exercise. Chemistry contexts supply all definitions, inputs, constants, units, and calculation relationships. For example, percentage yield means 100 times the collected mass divided by a supplied maximum possible mass. You are practising data handling and interpretation, not deriving a chemical reaction. Where a practical offers a choice of biological or organic-laboratory data, complete one route rather than treating both as additional required reports.

title: What you will learn and how to work
section: A lesson is a study unit, not a full day of new lectures
text:
A lesson is a study unit, not a full day of new lectures
Use each topic’s Lecture (slides) for the explanation and worked visual examples, then open Practical and notes for the complete instructions and saved deliverable. Slides use the arrow keys or navigation controls; return to the practical using the link in the deck. Each week has a short self-check quiz with explanations, for practice rather than an additional examination.
The numbered lessons suggest a five-week progression. Spend substantial time running examples, explaining results, recovering from mistakes, and returning to work after closing the applications. The exact contact timetable is arranged by the teaching team. If an installation fails, ask for support rather than spending the whole study unit trying unrelated system changes.
For most R lessons, a useful working rhythm is:

Open the course .Rproj and yesterday’s source file.
Read the biological question and identify what one row represents.
Predict a small example, run it, and explain the result.
Complete the practical, using hints and references as needed.
Save code, a plot or report, and a short interpretation.
Close/restart, reopen the work, and check that you can regenerate it.

What to keep
Preserve the raw data. Save R code or .Rmd source, not only a screenshot or printed number. Keep generated figures and HTML reports with their source and use the supported backup storage. Most daily exercises name a specific file to leave with; these are practice outputs, not a grading scheme.
The downloads page supplies datasets and a working report template. Reports are .Rmd files; the course website uses Quarto, which you do not need to author. We initially render HTML to keep the software setup small.

Getting help

Start at Day 1 or return to the five-week route.

title: Remote Linux: SSH and remote desktop
text: We will also use HPC2N or another remote Linux environment. A remote computer is a computer you connect to over the network. Your laptop displays the session; the remote computer runs the programs and stores the files you save there.

title: Remote Linux: SSH and remote desktop
section: Two ways to work remotely
text:
Two ways to work remotely








Connection
What you see
What you use it for




SSH
A terminal on the remote computer
Navigate folders and run commands.


Remote desktop
A graphical workspace on the remote computer
Use a file manager and the applications provided for the course.



Both give access to a remote environment. Whether they share exactly the same files depends on how the service is configured; the course instructions will identify the folders to use.

title: Remote Linux: SSH and remote desktop
section: What SSH means
text:
What SSH means
SSH is a way to log in securely to another computer. The usual command has this shape:
ssh your-username@remote-computer-address
This is an explanation of the shape, not a working course command. We will supply the actual address and explain any additional authentication steps.
On Windows you can start SSH from Ubuntu; on Mac use Terminal. Once connected, commands such as pwd and ls act on the remote computer. Use exit to leave the SSH session and return to your local shell.
The first connection may ask you to trust the remote computer’s host key. Follow the course’s verification instructions before accepting it. Password prompts may show no characters while you type. Never share passwords or authentication codes.

title: Remote Linux: SSH and remote desktop
section: Always ask: which computer am I using?
text:
Always ask: which computer am I using?







Question
Why it matters




Is this terminal local or remote?
It determines where commands run.


Which folder am I in?
pwd gives the location on that computer.


Where did I save the data or report?
Saving remotely does not automatically create a laptop copy.


Where is RStudio running?
R needs access to files in its own environment.



A browser download on your laptop, a file in local Ubuntu, and a file on HPC2N can be three separate copies. Identical filenames do not make them the same file. Opening a remote desktop does not automatically transfer your laptop’s files.

title: Remote Linux: SSH and remote desktop
section: What we will practise when access is ready
text:
What we will practise when access is ready

Sign in using the supplied instructions and identify the remote computer.
Use pwd and ls, create a practice folder, and locate a supplied dataset.
Leave the SSH session with exit, then reconnect and find the folder again.
Open the supported remote desktop and find the designated course files.
Transfer a small file using the supported route and identify both copies.
Open the provided R environment and locate a rendered report.

Download

title: R reference: the small vocabulary we use
text: These examples assume that you opened the extracted course .Rproj file. Use RStudio’s R console for R, not a terminal waiting for shell commands. Save reusable code in an R script or your .Rmd report.

title: R reference: the small vocabulary we use
section: Objects and functions
text:
Objects and functions
lengths_mm <- c(12, 15, 18)
mean(lengths_mm)
sd(lengths_mm)
length(lengths_mm)
<- assigns a value to a name. c() combines values into a vector. mean() computes an arithmetic mean, sd() a sample standard deviation, and length() the number of elements. Text needs quotes, as in "control". R is case-sensitive: Length and length are different names.

title: R reference: the small vocabulary we use
section: Import, inspect, and calculate
text:
Import, inspect, and calculate
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

seedlings <- read_csv("data/seedlings.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
head(seedlings)
names(seedlings)
nrow(seedlings)
glimpse(seedlings)

seedlings <- seedlings |>
  mutate(growth_mm = final_mm - initial_mm)
|> means “take this result and pass it to the next function”. mutate() adds or changes columns. A calculation creates a derived measurement; it does not change the original CSV unless you explicitly write a file.
treated <- seedlings |>
  filter(treatment == "treated")

summary_table <- seedlings |>
  group_by(treatment) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean_mm = mean(growth_mm), sd_mm = sd(growth_mm),
            .groups = "drop")
== compares values; it does not assign. filter() selects rows. group_by() tells summarise() which groups to summarise. For missing data, report both available and missing counts rather than silently dropping records.

title: R reference: the small vocabulary we use
section: A plot and an exported file
text:
A plot and an exported file
growth_plot <- ggplot(seedlings, aes(x = treatment, y = growth_mm)) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = 0.08, height = 0, seed = 7)) +
  labs(x = "Allocation", y = "Seven-day growth (mm)") +
  theme_minimal()
growth_plot
ggsave("output/growth.png", plot = growth_plot, width = 6, height = 4, dpi = 150)
write_csv(summary_table, "output/growth-summary.csv")
The + joins layers in a ggplot. Horizontal jitter separates overlapping points; height = 0 preserves their measured values. ggsave() needs an output folder that already exists; the course project includes one.

title: R reference: the small vocabulary we use
section: Missing is not zero
text:
Missing is not zero
x <- c(10, NA, 20)
is.na(x)
sum(is.na(x))
sum(!is.na(x))
mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)
NA denotes an unavailable value. na.rm = TRUE computes from available observations; it does not justify missingness or replace a report of how many were missing. The mean here is 15 from two available values.

title: R reference: the small vocabulary we use
section: Error recovery
text:
Error recovery







Message or symptom
Check




“object not found”
Spelling, case, and whether the line creating it ran


“could not find function”
Whether the right package was loaded


“cannot open file”
Project, path, filename case, and local versus remote computer


Console prompt is +
Unfinished quotes/brackets; press Esc and fix the expression


Report fails but console works
An object or package may exist only in your interactive session



Use ?mean, ?t.test, or ?lm to open R’s help for a named function. Ask for help with the exact error and the smallest relevant code, without credentials.

title: Terminal reference: find, inspect, and package files
text:
Use Ubuntu on Windows, Terminal on Mac, or the terminal provided remotely. Do not type the prompt ($ or %). Commands act on the computer to which the current shell belongs. Type pwd whenever you are unsure where you are.
Some commands overwrite existing files. Practise in the course workspace and read the destination name before pressing Enter. We do not need recursive deletion commands for the core practicals.

title: Terminal reference: find, inspect, and package files
section: Paths and punctuation
text:
Paths and punctuation
~                        your home folder on this computer
.                        the current folder
..                       the parent folder
data/seedlings.csv       a relative path from the current folder
/home/anna/course        an example absolute path on Linux
cd .. moves one level up. A filename containing spaces needs quoting, for example less "field notes.txt". Use simple filenames with hyphens or underscores in your own work. Use Tab to complete names and the up arrow to recall a command. Ctrl+C interrupts a running command; it is not the copy shortcut.

title: Terminal reference: find, inspect, and package files
section: A pipe connects programs
text:
A pipe connects programs
grep -F treated samples.tsv | wc -l
grep outputs matching lines. The | passes those lines to wc as input. There is no intermediate saved file. In our manifest, the answer is 2 because two records contain treated. This count is meaningful because each record is one line and the header does not contain the search term.

title: Terminal reference: find, inspect, and package files
section: Redirection saves output
text:
Redirection saves output
grep -F treated samples.tsv > treated-samples.txt
The > writes to a file instead of the screen and replaces existing contents at that path. >> appends, but we do not need it for this practical. The search does not parse a table or understand treatment groups: it matches text. It would also match untreated if that label occurred in the file.

title: Terminal reference: find, inspect, and package files
section: Connect graphical and terminal views
text:
Connect graphical and terminal views
In Ubuntu on Windows, explorer.exe . opens the current folder in File Explorer. On a Mac, open . opens it in Finder. These are local conveniences, not remote file-transfer commands. The remote desktop and file-transfer instructions will identify the supported remote route.
See week 1 for guided practice and remote access for the local/remote distinction.

title: Day 2 — Folders, paths, and the working computer
section: Start by finding yesterday’s work
text:
Start by finding yesterday’s work
Open the file manager and find day01-notes.txt using the folders, rather than the editor’s recent-file list. Tell a partner which route you took. Being able to explain where a file lives will help when your analysis later reports “file not found”.
Our biological question is still about seedling growth. Today we organise the experiment so that someone else can identify the original observations and the results we produce from them.

title: Day 2 — Folders, paths, and the working computer
section: Folders form a tree
text:
Folders form a tree
A folder can contain files and more folders. We can draw part of our project as a tree. Indentation shows what is inside what:
introcomputing-course/
├── introcomputing.Rproj
├── report.Rmd
├── data/
│   ├── README.md
│   └── seedlings.csv
├── output/
│   └── seedlings-practice.csv
└── reports/
    └── day01-notes.txt
This drawing omits other supplied datasets. data and reports are neighbours: neither is inside the other. Their parent folder is introcomputing-course. That folder is the project root because it is the starting point for this project’s organisation. It is not the root of the entire computer.
In the file manager, open reports, go up to its parent, and then enter data. Watch the address bar on Windows or the folder path in Finder. In Finder, View → Show Path Bar can make the route easier to see.

title: Day 2 — Folders, paths, and the working computer
section: A path gives the route to a file
text:
A path gives the route to a file
A path describes a location. These examples are illustrations: your username and exact Documents location will differ.
Windows: C:\Users\anna\Documents\introcomputing-course\data\seedlings.csv
Mac:     /Users/anna/Documents/introcomputing-course/data/seedlings.csv
Linux:   /home/anna/introcomputing-course/data/seedlings.csv
An absolute path starts from the file system’s root or drive and specifies the whole route. A relative path starts from an agreed current folder. From inside introcomputing-course, data/seedlings.csv means “enter data, then find seedlings.csv”. From inside reports, that same relative path would ask for a data folder inside reports, where it does not exist.
This is why we need to know our current working directory: the folder from which a program interprets relative paths. Next lesson we will ask the terminal to print it. Relative paths will let us move a whole project without changing every filename in the analysis.

title: Day 2 — Folders, paths, and the working computer
section: Practical 1: give directions through the tree
text:
Practical 1: give directions through the tree
Work in pairs. One person has the file-manager window; the other gives directions.

Start in the project root. Find the original seedling table.
Start in reports. Find the practice copy in output.
Return to the project root. Create a folder called practice.
Inside it, create field-notes and figures.
Copy yesterday’s note into field-notes and rename the copy seedling-observations.txt.
Draw the new part of the tree on paper. Swap roles and navigate from the drawing alone.

Prefer informative names with simple letters, numbers, and hyphens for this course. seedling-observations.txt is easier to interpret than new2.txt. We will learn to handle spaces too; simple names reduce avoidable typing errors.






I moved the whole project and now see two copies





First locate each copy and inspect its contents. A copy operation leaves the original in place; a move changes the location. Ask the teacher to help choose one working project before continuing. Do not delete a folder merely because its name looks similar to another.

title: Day 2 — Folders, paths, and the working computer
section: What happens when you open a file?
text:
What happens when you open a file?
Your laptop has several parts with different jobs:







Part
Job in our seedling example




Storage, such as an SSD
Holds the saved CSV and report between sessions.


Memory, or RAM
Holds information the running application is using now.


Processor, or CPU
Carries out instructions, such as calculating increases.


Operating system
Manages files, memory, devices, and running programs; Windows, macOS, and Linux are examples.


Application
Provides a particular tool, such as an editor, browser, or RStudio.



Opening a CSV lets an application read its saved contents. Editing text changes the application’s current working version. Saving writes that version to a file. An unsaved change may disappear when an application closes, even though the previously saved file remains. A process is a running instance of a program. An application installed on storage and a process using memory are related but different things.

title: Day 2 — Folders, paths, and the working computer
section: Practical 2: test the difference between editing and saving
text:
Practical 2: test the difference between editing and saving
Use practice/field-notes/seedling-observations.txt, not the original note.

Open the practice note and add “The plants were measured twice.”
Save, close, and reopen it. Confirm that the sentence remains.
Add “This line is an unsaved experiment.” Close the editor and choose to discard the change if asked. Reopen the file and inspect the result.

Some editors save automatically or restore unsaved documents. If yours restores the sentence, discuss that behaviour with a teacher rather than treating it as proof that saving never matters. The important check is what is actually in the saved file, and where the editor saved it.

title: Day 2 — Folders, paths, and the working computer
section: Where do local, cloud, and remote files live?
text:
Where do local, cloud, and remote files live?
A local file is on the computer you are using. A cloud service may keep a copy elsewhere and synchronise it with your laptop. A remote Linux computer is another computer we will log into. Its home folder is separate from yours. Opening its desktop does not automatically copy your downloads to it.
An archive in the same folder as the originals is convenient for sharing, but it is not protection against losing the whole laptop. Keep another copy using the university’s supported backup or storage service once the teaching team identifies it. Check that a copy completed and that you can retrieve it.

title: Day 2 — Folders, paths, and the working computer
section: Check your understanding
text:
Check your understanding






From the project root, what is the relative path to yesterday’s note?





reports/day01-notes.txt. From inside reports, its name alone is sufficient: day01-notes.txt. The file did not move; your starting location changed.









Does more RAM automatically provide more room for saved photographs?





No. RAM supports running work; persistent storage holds saved files. They have different jobs. We will see this again when R objects disappear after restarting R but the saved data file is still present.



Save today: add reports/day02-map.txt with a simple folder tree, the path to seedlings.csv, and one sentence distinguishing RAM from storage. Keep the practice folder for later navigation exercises.
Next: navigate these ideas in a terminal.

title: Day 4 — Unpack and inspect laboratory data
section: Which seedlings received the treatment?
text:
Which seedlings received the treatment?
A lab partner has sent a small archive containing measurements and sample information. Before doing statistics, we need to establish what is in the archive and which files belong to the treated samples. We will do this with ordinary command-line utilities. The data are simulated for teaching.
The archive in this exercise is a small separate practice dataset with four samples. It is not the 24-plant dataset we will analyse in R. A manifest is a table describing which samples and files are present. Sample identifiers connect the manifest to the measurements.

title: Day 4 — Unpack and inspect laboratory data
section: Put the download in a known place
text:
Put the download in a known place

Download lab-data.zip with your browser.
Locate the downloaded file in File Explorer or Finder.
In your terminal, run cd ~/introcomputing-shell, then pwd.
Open that folder graphically using explorer.exe . in local Ubuntu on Windows or open . on Mac.
Copy the downloaded ZIP into this workspace using the file manager. Do not assume your Windows browser downloaded it into Ubuntu’s home folder.
Back in the terminal, run ls. Confirm that lab-data.zip appears.

On a remote computer, use the course’s supported transfer route when available. The browser’s local download is not automatically a remote file.

title: Day 4 — Unpack and inspect laboratory data
section: Look before extracting
text:
Look before extracting
From ~/introcomputing-shell, run:
unzip -l lab-data.zip
The -l option lists archive contents without extracting them. Identify README.txt, samples.tsv, and the measurements and field-notes folders. There should be four measurement files, S01 through S04. The displayed sizes and dates are information about the archive entries; do not type them.
Now extract:
unzip lab-data.zip -d lab-data
cd lab-data
ls
less README.txt
The -d lab-data option chooses the destination folder. Extraction creates ordinary files you can open; it does not remove the ZIP. In less, use Space to move down, arrow keys to move by lines, and q to quit and return to the prompt. A short file may already fit on one screen.






Extraction asks whether to replace a file





You have probably extracted into the same destination before. Stop and inspect the destination in the file manager. For this first run, choose a fresh destination name if necessary and use that name in cd. Do not automatically agree to replace files that may contain your work.

title: Day 4 — Unpack and inspect laboratory data
section: Read a table without changing it
text:
Read a table without changing it
Run:
head -n 3 samples.tsv
wc -l samples.tsv
head -n 3 prints the first three lines. wc -l counts newline-terminated lines. The supplied manifest has a header and four sample records, so the count is 5, not four biological samples. Tabs separate the columns in this TSV (tab-separated values) file. A CSV uses commas instead.
The columns are sample_id, treatment, and file. Follow the file path for sample S03:
head measurements/S03.csv
Before interpreting a number, use the README to find out what it measures and which units were used. The filename locates measurements; it does not explain their biological meaning by itself.

title: Day 4 — Unpack and inspect laboratory data
section: Search the manifest with grep
text:
Search the manifest with grep
Run:
grep -F treated samples.tsv
grep prints lines matching a search. -F asks for a literal text match, so we do not need to learn pattern syntax. The supplied manifest should return two lines, S03 and S04, labelled treated.
This is text search, not an understanding of table columns or experiments. Searching for treated would also match untreated if that word were present. Our prepared labels are control and treated; the header does not contain the search word. Always inspect what a search actually selected.

title: Day 4 — Unpack and inspect laboratory data
section: Save a search, then count its records
text:
Save a search, then count its records
grep -F treated samples.tsv > treated-samples.txt
less treated-samples.txt
grep -F treated samples.tsv | wc -l
> redirects the output to a file instead of displaying it. It replaces the contents if that output file already exists. Never use the input filename on the right side here. treated-samples.txt is a new text extract; the original samples.tsv remains unchanged. It has no header, because the header did not match our search.
The vertical bar | is a pipe. It passes the matching lines from grep to wc -l, which counts them. The result should be 2. The pipe does not need an intermediate saved file. Count lines only when lines really represent the records you intend to count.

title: Day 4 — Unpack and inspect laboratory data
section: Practical: preserve and organise a working copy
text:
Practical: preserve and organise a working copy
Still inside lab-data, run:
mkdir working
cp samples.tsv working/samples-copy.tsv
mv working/samples-copy.tsv working/manifest-practice.tsv
ls working
cp creates a copy; mv moves or renames an entry. Here only the practice copy was renamed. Confirm that the original samples.tsv still exists. Both commands can replace existing destinations, so check names before running them.
Use the file manager to create observations.txt inside working. Record: how many sample records there are, which two received treatment, and which measurement file you would open for S04. Add the distinction between the five manifest lines and the four samples.

title: Day 4 — Unpack and inspect laboratory data
section: A first look at the remote computer
text:
A first look at the remote computer
The teacher will demonstrate SSH and remote desktop. SSH gives a terminal on another computer. A remote desktop gives a graphical workspace there. In either case, saved files can be on that other computer, even while your laptop displays the session.
When account details are available, follow the supplied instructions and try pwd and ls remotely. State aloud: “This command runs on ; this path is on .” If accounts are not ready, continue the local practical. Do not guess a login address.

title: Day 4 — Unpack and inspect laboratory data
section: Check your understanding
text:
Check your understanding






Did grep change the manifest? Why does wc -l sometimes count a header?





grep reads the file; redirection saved its output separately. wc -l counts lines, not their meaning. The full manifest includes a header, while our saved matching lines do not. We must know the file’s structure to interpret the count.



Save today: treated-samples.txt, working/manifest-practice.tsv, and working/observations.txt in the extracted lab-data folder. Be able to show where the untouched archive and manifest are located.
Next: repeat the workflow and package your findings.

text: Try each question before opening its answer. These are practice checks, not graded examination questions. Use your file manager, terminal, and terminal reference to check actions as well as words.

title: Week 1 self-check — files and computers
section: 1. Find the saved work
text:
1. Find the saved work
You edited a note in an application, closed it, and cannot find it in the application’s recent-files list. What should you be able to identify, and why does the application name alone not tell you where the file is?






Answer and check





Identify the computer, folder, and filename where the note was saved. An application can open files from many locations. Navigate to the saved folder in the file manager and reopen the ordinary file. If the changes were not saved, the saved contents may differ from the previous screen.

title: Week 1 self-check — files and computers
section: 2. A relative path needs a starting place
text:
2. A relative path needs a starting place
From introcomputing-course, the path data/seedlings.csv works. From inside reports, why does the same path ask for a different location?






Answer and check





A relative path starts at the current folder. From reports it asks for reports/data/seedlings.csv, not the neighbouring data folder. Return to the project root, then locate data/seedlings.csv. The file did not move; your starting location changed. In a shell, use pwd to identify that starting place.

title: Week 1 self-check — files and computers
section: 3. Predict a pipe and a saved extract
text:
3. Predict a pipe and a saved extract
The supplied samples.tsv has a header plus four records: two control and two treated. The header does not contain treated. What does this print, and does the second command change the source manifest?
grep -F treated samples.tsv | wc -l
grep -F treated samples.tsv > treated-samples.txt






Answer and check





The first command prints a line count of 2. grep sends matching lines through the pipe to wc. The second saves matches to treated-samples.txt; it does not change samples.tsv. > replaces any previous contents of the destination. This is literal text matching, not interpretation of treatment groups or chemical classes. It could also match untreated if that word occurred.

title: Week 1 self-check — files and computers
section: 4. Copy, move, and extract
text:
4. Copy, move, and extract
What remains after copying notes.txt to notes-copy.txt? How is moving the original different? Does opening a ZIP preview necessarily mean its files have been extracted into an ordinary project folder?






Answer and check





A copy leaves the original and makes another file. A move changes the original’s location or name. A ZIP preview is a view of an archive; use extraction to create the ordinary folder and files needed for the project. Locate the actual extracted .Rproj, rather than opening one inside an archive preview.

title: Week 1 self-check — files and computers
section: 5. Memory and storage
text:
5. Memory and storage
Would adding RAM automatically provide more room for saved photographs? Why can restarting R remove objects while leaving a saved CSV intact?






Answer and check





RAM supports running work; persistent storage holds saved files. They have different roles. An R object in session memory must be recreated after restart; the CSV remains on storage and can be imported again. Saving a script preserves the instructions, not an automatically running process.

title: Week 1 self-check — files and computers
section: 6. The same filename on two computers
text:
6. The same filename on two computers
You see report.html in a remote desktop. Is it automatically in your laptop’s Downloads folder? Would a ZIP stored beside the original be a separate backup against losing the laptop?






Answer and check





No to both. Remote access is not automatic file transfer, and identical names can refer to separate copies. Use the supported transfer route and name the destination. A ZIP on the same disk is a convenient sharing package; use supported separate storage for protection against losing that disk.



Return to day 5 practical for a complete file workflow, or continue to week 2.

title: Day 7 — Read a table and find out what it means
section: Today’s question
text:
Today’s question
We have lengths from 24 seedlings. Twelve independently potted plants were randomly assigned to a control group and twelve to a treatment group. Each plant was measured at the beginning and end of the same observation period. Can we bring the measurements into R without losing their meaning?
Open introcomputing.Rproj in the extracted course folder. Its data/ subfolder contains the supplied files and a README.md explaining them. A CSV is a text file in which commas separate columns. Its first line is a header naming those columns. The file is storage; importing creates an R object in memory.

title: Day 7 — Read a table and find out what it means
section: Start from a known place
text:
Start from a known place
Create day07.R in the project root. Run:

getwd()
file.exists("data/seedlings.csv")

getwd() reports R’s working directory. It should be your extracted project folder, not the data folder. The second line should return TRUE. The relative path data/seedlings.csv means “inside data, find seedlings.csv, starting here”. Your full home-folder path differs from a classmate’s; this relative path can stay the same when they open their own project.
If file.exists() returns FALSE, inspect the folder in the file manager. A common problem is opening the ZIP rather than an extracted project, or an extra folder layer. Avoid solving this by inserting your personal absolute path into every line of code. Open the correct project instead.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 7 — Read a table and find out what it means
section: Import and inspect
text:
Import and inspect
The readr package provides a table importer. Packages add functions to R; installing a package puts it on disk, while library() loads it for this session. The software setup page explains installation. Loading is needed again after restarting R.

library(readr)
seedlings <- read_csv("data/seedlings.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
head(seedlings)
dim(seedlings)
names(seedlings)
str(seedlings)

read_csv() returns a table, displayed as a tibble. head() shows its first rows, not the complete dataset. dim() gives 24 rows and 4 columns. names() returns column names. str() describes structure and types: plant_id and treatment are text; the two lengths are numeric. Suppressing the type message with show_col_types = FALSE does not remove the need to check types.
Read the first row aloud: plant P01 is in the control group; its initial length was 25.7 mm and its final length 44.3 mm. Each row represents one plant, each column one variable. Two lengths from the same row are measurements on the same plant, not two independent plants.

seedlings$initial_mm
length(seedlings$initial_mm)
mean(seedlings$initial_mm)

$ selects a named column from the table, giving a vector. The length is 24. A mean without a unit is incomplete: the average initial length is measured in mm. The numbers cannot tell you whether the file used mm or cm; the dictionary and measurement protocol provide that information.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 7 — Read a table and find out what it means
section: Missing is different from zero
text:
Missing is different from zero
A missing measurement is represented by NA after import. NA means not available. It does not mean zero length, no growth, or a control treatment.

example_mm <- c(12, NA, 18)
mean(example_mm)
mean(example_mm, na.rm = TRUE)
is.na(example_mm)

The first mean is NA: R will not silently pretend all measurements are known. The second is 15 mm, calculated from two observed values. na.rm = TRUE requests omitting missing values for this calculation. A report must still explain how many observations were missing and why, if known.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 7 — Read a table and find out what it means
section: Your practical
text:
Your practical

Import seedlings.csv and save the import and inspection commands in day07.R.
Record in comments the row count, column count, column meanings, and units.
Inspect tail(seedlings) to see the last rows. Find P24 and its treatment.
Use sum(is.na(seedlings$final_mm)) to count missing final measurements.
Import data/leaf-mass.csv into leaves, inspect it, and use its dictionary to explain what one row represents. Do not assume it has the seedling columns.
Restart R and run your script from the top. The raw CSV files should remain exactly as supplied.







Hint: a function is not found





Run library(readr) before read_csv(). If loading fails because the package is not installed, use the setup instructions or ask for help. For column names, copy from names(seedlings); initial_mm and initial are different names.

title: Day 7 — Read a table and find out what it means
section: Check your understanding
text:
Check your understanding
Why is the header not a plant? Why does the file’s name not tell R the units? Why should the script work from a classmate’s project folder?






Check your answers





The header labels columns rather than containing an observation. Units are metadata supplied by people; R only sees column names and values. The script uses relative paths and the same documented folder structure rather than your username. There are no missing final lengths in the clean seedling dataset.

title: Day 9 — Make a report that runs its own calculations
section: Today’s question
text:
Today’s question
Can someone read our explanation, inspect our calculation, and see the figure without copying results manually? An R Markdown report combines ordinary text with executable R code. Rendering turns that source document into a readable HTML report. An HTML report can be opened in a browser; the editable source ends in .Rmd and should be kept too.

Here is a minimal complete report. The three-backtick fences in the box belong in your .Rmd file.
---
title: "Seedling growth"
output: html_document
---

## Question

How much did the seedlings grow during the observation period?

```{r import}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
seedlings <- read_csv("data/seedlings.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
seedlings <- mutate(seedlings, growth_mm = final_mm - initial_mm)
```

There are `r nrow(seedlings)` plants in the dataset.

```{r mean-growth}
mean(seedlings$growth_mm)
```

Growth is final minus initial length, measured in millimetres.
