title: Day 12 — An average does not describe every plant
text: Lecture slides · Weekly self-check

title: Day 12 — An average does not describe every plant
section: Today’s question
text:
Today’s question
Two groups can have the same average growth yet look very different. How can we say where measurements are centred and how much individual plants vary? Today we use small numbers first, then connect them to the seedling experiment.

title: Day 12 — An average does not describe every plant
section: Mean and median answer slightly different questions
text:
Mean and median answer slightly different questions
The mean adds all observed values and divides by their number. The median is the middle of the ordered values, or the mean of the middle two for an even number of values. Both describe a centre; neither replaces the observations.

growth_mm <- c(12, 14, 16)
mean(growth_mm)
median(growth_mm)

Both results are 14 mm. Now inspect a more uneven set:

uneven_mm <- c(10, 10, 10, 100)
mean(uneven_mm)
median(uneven_mm)

The mean is 32.5 mm and median 10 mm. Neither is an arithmetic error. The large observation affects the mean strongly. Investigate whether a large value is supported by the source record; do not delete it simply to make the mean and median agree. The appropriate description depends on the question and shape of the measurements.

title: Day 12 — An average does not describe every plant
section: Variance measures spread around the mean
text:
Variance measures spread around the mean
For the three measurements 12, 14, and 16 mm, the deviations from their mean are −2, 0, and 2 mm. Their sum is zero, so an ordinary mean deviation would hide the spread. Squaring deviations prevents positive and negative values cancelling.
The sample variance adds squared deviations and divides by one less than the number of observations. The choice of this denominator helps estimate population variance from a sample; a derivation is beyond this course.

growth_mm <- c(12, 14, 16)
deviations_mm <- growth_mm - mean(growth_mm)
squared_deviations <- deviations_mm^2
sum(squared_deviations) / (length(growth_mm) - 1)
var(growth_mm)
sd(growth_mm)

The squared deviations are 4, 0, and 4. Their sum divided by 2 is 4 mm², the sample variance. The standard deviation, or SD, is its square root: 2 mm. SD is expressed in the original measurement’s units, which makes it easier to interpret alongside the mean. Variance uses squared units. Neither is the error in the mean or a claim that every plant lies within one SD.

close_mm <- c(13, 14, 15)
spread_mm <- c(8, 14, 20)
mean(close_mm)
mean(spread_mm)
sd(close_mm)
sd(spread_mm)

Both means are 14 mm. The SDs are 1 and 6 mm. The second set varies more among observations. A group with larger spread is not automatically measured less carefully: organisms can really differ. Measurement noise and biological variation can both contribute to observed spread.



Two toy groups share a mean of 14 mm but differ in spread. Dots are measurements; the dashed line is their common mean.

title: Day 12 — An average does not describe every plant
section: Apply the descriptions to plants
text:
Apply the descriptions to plants
Use the clean supplied table today so that variation is not confused with the repair exercise. Recreate all prerequisites in day12-variation.R.

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
seedlings <- read_csv("data/seedlings.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(growth_mm = final_mm - initial_mm)
control <- filter(seedlings, treatment == "control")
mean(control$growth_mm)
median(control$growth_mm)
var(control$growth_mm)
sd(control$growth_mm)

The control mean is about 15.3 mm and its SD about 3.19 mm. Report them with units and a sensible number of decimals; extra decimal places do not create more precise measurements. R may display more digits to help calculation, but those are not a requirement for prose.

title: Day 12 — An average does not describe every plant
section: Your practical
text:
Your practical

Work through the three-measurement variance by hand, then compare with R.
Predict the mean and SD if every value in close_mm increases by 10 mm. Check using mean(close_mm + 10) and sd(close_mm + 10).
Predict what happens if lengths are converted from mm to cm by dividing by ten. Check the mean, variance, and SD in the new units.
Calculate the treated group’s mean, median, variance, and SD. Write two sentences comparing centre and spread with the control group. The teacher may substitute the organic-laboratory transfer task below for this step; you do not need to complete both.
Add a note explaining why “the average plant grew 15.3 mm” does not mean every control plant grew exactly that amount.

title: Day 12 — An average does not describe every plant
section: Transfer choice: variation in collected product
text:
Transfer choice: variation in collected product
An organic synthesis is an experiment intended to make a product. In our simulated data/organic-recovery.csv, each row is one independent run. The supplied theoretical mass is the maximum product mass possible from that run’s starting materials; you do not need to derive it. Isolated mass is the dry product actually collected, assumed pure for this simplified calculation. Both are in grams. Calculate percentage yield as 100 × isolated mass / theoretical mass.

organic <- read_csv("data/organic-recovery.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(yield_percent = 100 * isolated_mass_g / theoretical_mass_g)
standard_runs <- filter(organic, protocol == "standard")
mean(standard_runs$yield_percent)
var(standard_runs$yield_percent)
sd(standard_runs$yield_percent)

Y01 gives 100 × 0.62 / 1.00 = 62%. For the six standard-protocol runs, the mean is about 68.67%, variance 18.67 squared percentage points, and SD 4.32 percentage points. A difference from 62% to 70% is eight percentage points, not an eight-percent relative increase. Repeat the summaries for the modified protocol and describe centre and spread in two sentences.
The runs used different starting amounts, so raw collected grams do not make the same comparison as percentage yield. A higher yield alone does not establish greater purity or a generally better method. Save this calculation in today’s script; no knowledge of reaction mechanisms is needed.






Hint: use the units to check yourself





Adding a constant shifts the centre but leaves deviations unchanged. Dividing lengths by ten divides the mean and SD by ten, but divides variance by one hundred. Check ?var and ?sd for the functions’ definitions and missing-value arguments.

title: Day 12 — An average does not describe every plant
section: Check your understanding
text:
Check your understanding






Which spread is larger?





The treated SD is about 4.87 mm, larger than the control SD. This describes variation among these plants; it does not by itself quantify uncertainty in the difference between group means. We will separate those questions next.



Keep: day12-variation.R and the interpretation in comments or report notes. Next: summarise groups while still showing individuals.

title: Day 14 — More readings are not always more independent evidence
text: Lecture slides · Weekly self-check

title: Day 14 — More readings are not always more independent evidence
section: Today’s question
text:
Today’s question
Would measuring the same plant ten times tell us as much about other plants as measuring ten different plants? The answer changes how we count evidence and interpret an average. Today is about experimental reasoning, supported by a small simulation provided for you to run. You do not need to write simulations.

title: Day 14 — More readings are not always more independent evidence
section: Identify what was independently sampled or treated
text:
Identify what was independently sampled or treated
In the seedling experiment, plants are grown in separate pots and treatment is randomly assigned to plants. The plant is our independent experimental unit. An independent biological replicate provides another unit relevant to the question. A technical replicate repeats measurement of the same material, helping reveal measurement variation.
Three ruler readings of P01 can help assess how consistently it was measured. They do not turn it into three independently treated plants. Similarly, 100 cells from one organism are not automatically 100 independent organisms, and ten time points from one culture are not ten independent cultures. The unit follows the design and biological question, not the number of rows in a spreadsheet.
Imagine a nutrient treatment assigned to two trays, each holding twelve plants. If each tray receives a single shared treatment, the tray is a treatment unit. Treating all 24 plants as independently randomised units would overstate the independent treatment information. More data rows cannot repair that design.

title: Day 14 — More readings are not always more independent evidence
section: Spread among plants versus uncertainty in a mean
text:
Spread among plants versus uncertainty in a mean
SD describes how much measured plants vary. Sampling uncertainty concerns how our estimated mean would change if we repeated the sampling process. Even when a population’s spread stays the same, a mean based on more independent plants typically varies less from sample to sample.
Here is a teacher-provided demonstration. The clean seedling growth measurements serve as a fixed toy population for repeated sampling. This is not a new experiment and is not evidence about all plants in nature. Sampling with replacement is used to illustrate repeated draws from a fixed distribution.
Save the block in day14-sampling.R, then run it unchanged first:

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
seedlings <- read_csv("data/seedlings.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(growth_mm = final_mm - initial_mm)
population_mm <- seedlings$growth_mm
set.seed(14)
means_4 <- replicate(400, mean(sample(population_mm, size = 4, replace = TRUE)))
means_16 <- replicate(400, mean(sample(population_mm, size = 16, replace = TRUE)))
sampling <- data.frame(mean_mm = c(means_4, means_16),
                       sample_size = rep(c("4 plants", "16 plants"), each = 400))
ggplot(sampling, aes(x = mean_mm)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, colour = "white") +
  facet_wrap(~ sample_size, ncol = 1) +
  labs(x = "Mean growth in one simulated sample (mm)",
       y = "Number of simulated samples") +
  theme_minimal()
sd(population_mm)
sd(means_4)
sd(means_16)

sample() draws a sample; replicate() repeats the calculation 400 times. replace = TRUE allows a source value to be drawn more than once. set.seed() sets the starting state of the random-number generator so the demonstration can be repeated exactly. The resulting 400 means are summaries of simulated samples, not 400 newly measured plants.
Notice the horizontal axis: each value is a sample mean. Compare its spread between sample sizes. Do not confuse sd(means_16) with SD among the 16 plants inside one particular sample. The former describes variation among repeated estimates and approximates a standard error in this toy sampling process.

title: Day 14 — More readings are not always more independent evidence
section: Your practical
text:
Your practical



Repeated sample means from samples of sixteen plants cluster more tightly than means from samples of four. The source distribution is fixed in this toy demonstration.



Before running the demonstration, predict which sample means will spread out more. Compare the plot and printed SDs with your prediction.
Change the random seed to 25 and rerun. Exact bins change; does the main relationship between sample size and spread remain?
Draw a small diagram for each design: twelve independent pots; one pot with twelve ruler readings; two trays with twelve plants each and tray-level treatment. Label the unit assigned to treatment. As an alternative to the one-pot diagram, draw one synthesis run whose collected product is weighed twelve times: there is one independently prepared run, not twelve. In the simulated organic dataset, six separately prepared runs were randomly assigned to each protocol; those runs provide independent protocol units.
Write an explanation for a lab partner: “We have many measurements, but our number of independently treated units is …”. Complete it for each design.
Save a two-sentence explanation of the difference between SD among plants and uncertainty in a group mean for your report.







Hint: keep the sampling target fixed





Both means_4 and means_16 draw from the same population_mm. A larger sample does not alter those source values or their SD. It changes how much the repeated sample means vary. These combined-treatment values are only a teaching population; this simulation is not a treatment comparison.

title: Day 14 — More readings are not always more independent evidence
section: Check your understanding
text:
Check your understanding






Is a precise mean enough?





No. Repeated measurements may be biased, dependent, or drawn from an unrepresentative source. A narrow sampling distribution does not establish that the sampling process answers the intended biological question. Independent units and an appropriate design still matter.



Keep: day14-sampling.R, your replicate diagrams, and the two-sentence explanation. Next: write a descriptive report.

title: Week 3 self-check — measurements and variation
text: Explain the quantities before calculating. Use these checks to identify what to practise again; they are not an assessment. Keep the statistics reference nearby.

title: Week 3 self-check — measurements and variation
section: 1. Mean, variance, and SD
text:
1. Mean, variance, and SD
Three growth measurements are 12, 14, and 16 mm. What are the mean, sample variance, and sample SD? Show the units.






Worked answer





Mean = 14 mm. Deviations are −2, 0, and 2 mm; squared deviations sum to 8. Divide by n − 1 = 2 to obtain sample variance 4 mm². Its square root is sample SD 2 mm. SD describes spread among these measurements, not the uncertainty in their mean.

title: Week 3 self-check — measurements and variation
section: 2. A common shift and a unit conversion
text:
2. A common shift and a unit conversion
If every measurement above gains 10 mm, what happens to mean and SD? If the original lengths are converted from mm to cm, how do mean, SD, and variance change?






Answer and check





Adding 10 shifts the mean to 24 mm but leaves SD at 2 mm, since deviations from the mean are unchanged. Dividing lengths by ten gives mean 1.4 cm, SD 0.2 cm, and variance 0.04 cm². Variance scales by the square of the conversion factor.

title: Week 3 self-check — measurements and variation
section: 3. An unusual number is a question, not proof of an error
text:
3. An unusual number is a question, not proof of an error
The messy table contains final length 4.38 for P21. What permits correcting it to 43.8 mm? What should happen to the unavailable final measurement for P06?






Answer and check





The supplied source notes confirm a transcription/unit error and give 43.8 mm. The unusual value alone would not justify multiplying by ten. P06 remains missing because there is no supported replacement in this exercise. Preserve the raw file and record repairs in code; zero would invent a measurement.

title: Week 3 self-check — measurements and variation
section: 4. Rows versus available measurements
text:
4. Rows versus available measurements
After the confirmed identical duplicate is removed, the repaired table has 24 plants and one unavailable growth value in the control group. How many plant records and available growth measurements are there per group?






Answer and check





There are 12 control and 12 treated plant records, but 11 control and 12 treated available growth measurements. The complete clean seedling file used later is a separate teaching dataset with 12 available per group. State which file the analysis uses, and do not silently mix those counts.

title: Week 3 self-check — measurements and variation
section: 5. More readings or more independent units?
text:
5. More readings or more independent units?
One treated plant is measured twelve times. A second study independently assigns twelve plants to treatment. Are these equivalent sources of information about differences among plants?






Answer and check





No. Repeated readings of one plant may reveal measurement consistency but do not create twelve independently treated plants. The design determines the experimental unit. Likewise, reweighing one synthesis run does not create more independently prepared runs.

title: Week 3 self-check — measurements and variation
section: 6. Spread of observations versus spread of sample means
text:
6. Spread of observations versus spread of sample means
The supplied simulation draws means from samples of four or sixteen plants from the same fixed toy population. Why can the means of sixteen spread less without changing the population’s individual SD?






Answer and check





The source measurements stay the same. A mean averages independent sampling variation, so repeated means based on more observations typically vary less. The SD among repeated sample means describes sampling variability of an estimate; it is not SD among individual plants. A precise estimate can still be biased or based on an inappropriate design.



Return to the descriptive report, or continue to comparisons.

title: Day 17 — A guided Welch t-test
text: Lecture slides · Weekly self-check

title: Day 17 — A guided Welch t-test
section: Today’s question
text:
Today’s question
Our sample shows about 6.22 mm more growth in the treated group. How uncertain is that estimated difference, and how does the experiment compare with an equal-means model? We will add a Welch two-sample t-test to yesterday’s report. We use this method for two independent groups and do not require their variances to be equal.
Open the project and comparison.Rmd. Run its import and preparation chunks so that seedlings, treated, and control exist. All code needed to create these objects must remain in the report: a successful console session is not enough.

title: Day 17 — A guided Welch t-test
section: Check the design before calling a function
text:
Check the design before calling a function
Each value in treated is one plant’s growth; each value in control is another plant’s growth. The groups are independent, treatments were randomly assigned, and we have not selected plants according to whether their growth supports our expectations. Inspect yesterday’s plot for severe skew, questionable values, or one observation dominating a group. With small groups, these features can make the usual interval and test unreliable. Seek advice when the method looks unsuitable; do not delete valid extreme observations to improve a p-value.
The test does not repair dependence, biased sampling, or measurement errors. We are using a small, deliberately simple dataset to learn an analysis workflow.

title: Day 17 — A guided Welch t-test
section: Run the comparison in the direction we stated
text:
Run the comparison in the direction we stated

comparison <- t.test(treated, control, var.equal = FALSE,
                     alternative = "two.sided", conf.level = 0.95)
comparison

The first vector is treated, the second control. The confidence interval therefore describes treated minus control. var.equal = FALSE explicitly selects Welch’s method. The other arguments make our two-sided question and interval level visible. You can inspect arguments with ?t.test; the R documentation also describes the returned result.
For these simulated data, key parts of the output are approximately:
Welch Two Sample t-test
p-value = 0.001517
95 percent confidence interval:
 2.701  9.732
sample estimates:
mean of x  mean of y
 21.4917    15.2750
Small printing differences are normal. The t statistic and degrees of freedom are part of the calculation; you do not need to derive them here. Concentrate on the question, difference, interval, and assumptions.

title: Day 17 — A guided Welch t-test
section: Read the result in a useful order
text:
Read the result in a useful order
First state the estimated effect: treated plants grew on average 6.22 mm more than controls in our sample. Then state its 95% confidence interval: about 2.70 to 9.73 mm for the population mean difference, under the model assumptions.
The interval expresses uncertainty in a mean difference. It is not a range containing 95% of individual plants. A 95% confidence procedure would cover the true difference in about 95% of repeated experiments under its assumptions. This particular interval either covers that fixed difference or does not; we do not know which. Values near the interval’s centre fit the data better than more distant values, rather than all values in the interval being equally plausible.
Finally report the p-value, about 0.0015. An equal-means model would rarely produce a two-sided t statistic at least this extreme under the assumptions. This is evidence against equal population means in this model. It is not a 99.85% probability that the treatment works, and it does not tell us whether 6 mm matters biologically. That judgment needs the organism, duration, and purpose of the study.

title: Day 17 — A guided Welch t-test
section: Practical: extend your report
text:
Practical: extend your report
Add a Methods paragraph naming the two independent groups, growth calculation, direction of comparison, and Welch two-sample t-test. Keep the individual-point plot. Add the test chunk and a Results paragraph with the two means, sample sizes, estimated difference, interval, and p-value. A possible structure is:

In these simulated observations, mean growth was … in … and … in … . The estimated treated-minus-control difference was … mm (95% confidence interval … to … mm; Welch two-sample t-test, p = …). This suggests … under … .

Use your own words for the last sentence. Do not report only “significant”.
Extract numbers rather than retyping a long printout:

mean(treated) - mean(control)
comparison$conf.int
comparison$p.value

The $ selects a named component of the result. The interval’s two endpoints are the lower and upper limits in the direction we selected. If you later use a formula interface, check its group order carefully; the sign may reverse.






Hint: what if the interval includes zero?





Zero represents equal population means for this comparison. An interval spanning zero would show that the data do not resolve the direction at this confidence level. It would not establish equivalence or prove that there is no effect.

title: Day 17 — A guided Welch t-test
section: Check your understanding
text:
Check your understanding

Which has units of millimetres: the difference, the interval, or the p-value? The first two; a p-value has no measurement units.
Does group SD describe uncertainty in the difference? No; SD describes individual spread within a group.
If all these plants came from one shared pot per treatment, would the same analysis be justified? No; the independent-unit assumption would change.

title: Day 19 — A calibration line

title: Day 19 — A calibration line
section: Today’s question
text:
Today’s question
A laboratory instrument gives an absorbance reading, but we want a concentration. We first measure solutions of known concentration, called standards. Can a straight line describe their readings well enough to estimate the concentration of an unknown sample?
This is a common quantitative laboratory workflow. The prepared standards in data/calibration.csv cover 0–10 mg/L. Absorbance is dimensionless. These are simulated data for a simple teaching example; no particular reagent or actual assay is implied. Each standard is one calibration point, not a plant or a replicate treatment group.

title: Day 19 — A calibration line
section: Put known concentration on the horizontal axis
text:
Put known concentration on the horizontal axis

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

standards <- read_csv("data/calibration.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
calibration_plot <- ggplot(standards,
                          aes(x = concentration_mg_l, y = absorbance)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  labs(x = "Known concentration (mg/L)", y = "Absorbance") +
  theme_minimal()
calibration_plot

The readings increase approximately along a line. We describe that line as absorbance = intercept + slope × concentration. The intercept is the fitted reading at concentration zero. The slope is the fitted increase in absorbance for a one mg/L increase in concentration. A fitted line summarises the relation; it does not have to pass through every observation.

title: Day 19 — A calibration line
section: Fit the line in R
text:
Fit the line in R

calibration_fit <- lm(absorbance ~ concentration_mg_l, data = standards)
coef(calibration_fit)

lm() fits a linear model. In its formula, ~ separates the response on the left from the explanatory variable on the right. data = standards says where to find the columns. coef() extracts the fitted intercept and slope. The R documentation for lm is a reference; we use only this simple straight-line case.
Your fitted coefficients should be approximately 0.03957 for the intercept and 0.06489 for the slope. Thus the line is approximately absorbance = 0.03957 + 0.06489 × concentration.

calibration_plot <- calibration_plot +
  geom_abline(intercept = coef(calibration_fit)[1],
              slope = coef(calibration_fit)[2], colour = "steelblue")
calibration_plot

The [1] and [2] select the first and second coefficients. We retain the full-precision values for calculations; rounded values are useful for prose. The nonzero intercept may represent a background reading. Do not force the line through zero merely because concentration zero sounds like “nothing”.



Prepared standards and their fitted calibration line.

title: Day 19 — A calibration line
section: Check deviations from the line
text:
Check deviations from the line
A residual is an observed reading minus the line’s fitted reading. Positive means the point is above the line; negative means it is below. Residuals have absorbance units here.

standards <- standards |>
  mutate(fitted_absorbance = fitted(calibration_fit),
         residual = residuals(calibration_fit))
standards

residual_plot <- ggplot(standards,
                        aes(x = concentration_mg_l, y = residual)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  labs(x = "Known concentration (mg/L)", y = "Residual absorbance") +
  theme_minimal()
residual_plot




Deviations of standard readings from the fitted line, in absorbance units.


Look for curvature or a point that stands apart, not for all residuals to be positive or negative. These six small residuals show no obvious curved pattern. Six standards are still limited evidence: the picture does not guarantee that the relationship holds at arbitrary concentrations.

title: Day 19 — A calibration line
section: Estimate the unknowns within the calibration range
text:
Estimate the unknowns within the calibration range
Rearranging the line gives concentration = (absorbance − intercept) / slope. This is a point estimate; we are not calculating a full uncertainty interval for the unknown concentration.

unknowns <- read_csv("data/unknowns.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
intercept <- coef(calibration_fit)[1]
slope <- coef(calibration_fit)[2]

unknowns <- unknowns |>
  mutate(within_range = absorbance >= min(standards$absorbance) &
                        absorbance <= max(standards$absorbance),
         concentration_mg_l = if_else(
           within_range, (absorbance - intercept) / slope, NA_real_))
unknowns

The & requires both range conditions. if_else() assigns a numeric missing value, NA_real_, to unsupported estimates. U1 is about 4.17 mg/L and U2 about 7.40 mg/L. U3 exceeds the largest measured standard reading. Report it as outside the calibration range; do not present an extrapolated value as a valid result. A real laboratory might dilute the sample and measure it again using its assay protocol. Do not invent a dilution correction without such a measurement.

title: Day 19 — A calibration line
section: Transfer question: a newly measured dilution
text:
Transfer question: a newly measured dilution
Use this short calculation as a transfer check, rather than doing another complete calibration exercise. A dilution mixes some original solution with solvent to reach a larger final total volume. Assume that no measured substance is lost or reacts. Its concentration is reduced by the factor final total volume / original-sample volume.
A separate unknown was outside the instrument range. A new measurement is now provided: 1.00 mL of the original was diluted to a total of 10.00 mL, and the diluted reading was 0.520. This is not an instruction to add 10 mL of solvent, and it is not a new reading for U3. All data remain simulated.

Check that 0.520 is inside the measured standard-reading range.
Use the fitted line to calculate the diluted concentration in mg/L.
Multiply by 10.00 / 1.00 to estimate the original concentration.
State why this differs from extrapolating a line beyond its measured range.







Hint and numerical check





diluted_absorbance <- 0.520
dilution_factor <- 10.00 / 1.00
diluted_mg_l <- (diluted_absorbance - intercept) / slope
original_mg_l <- diluted_mg_l * dilution_factor
c(diluted_mg_l = diluted_mg_l, original_mg_l = original_mg_l)
Using unrounded coefficients, the estimates are about 7.40 mg/L diluted and 74.04 mg/L original. The diluted reading is within range; the original estimate follows from that new reading and a stated dilution factor. This does not make U3’s old out-of-range reading valid. Full measurement, dilution, and calibration uncertainty are still omitted from these point estimates.

title: Day 19 — A calibration line
section: Practical and saved work
text:
Practical and saved work
Create calibration-report.Rmd at the project root. Explain what a standard is, include the line and residual plots, describe the slope with units, and report the two supported concentration estimates. Explain why U3 needs another step. State that these simple inverse estimates omit full calibration uncertainty. Save the table with write_csv(unknowns, "output/day19-unknowns.csv") and both figures with ggsave(). Render after restarting R.






Hint: which way round is the model?





We prepared concentration and measured absorbance, so we fit absorbance as the response. We then rearrange that fitted line. Fitting concentration as a response is a different regression and is not the workflow used here.

title: Day 19 — A calibration line
section: Check your understanding
text:
Check your understanding

What does a positive residual mean? The observed reading is above the line.
Does a good fit from 0–10 mg/L justify a prediction at 100 mg/L? No.
Are concentration estimates exact? No; standards, measurement, and the fitted relationship all contribute uncertainty.

Leave with: the calibration report, supported concentration table, and figures.
Next: Day 20 — A biological association.

title: Week 4 self-check — comparisons and fitted lines
text: Use the stated design, units, and direction before interpreting output. These questions are formative and need no new statistical method. Refer to the statistics reference as needed.

title: Week 4 self-check — comparisons and fitted lines
section: 1. Interpret the direction and interval
text:
1. Interpret the direction and interval
For independent seedlings, the estimated treated-minus-control mean growth difference is 6.22 mm, with a 95% confidence interval from 2.70 to 9.73 mm. What quantity is this interval describing? Is it a range for 95% of the plants?






Answer





It describes uncertainty in the population mean difference, under the model assumptions and in the stated treated-minus-control direction. It is not a range containing 95% of individual plants. A 95% confidence procedure covers the fixed true quantity in about 95% of repeated samples when its assumptions hold.

title: Week 4 self-check — comparisons and fitted lines
section: 2. What does the p-value condition on?
text:
2. What does the p-value condition on?
Does a p-value of 0.0015 mean a 0.15% probability that the null hypothesis is true, or prove that a 6 mm difference matters biologically?






Answer





Neither. It describes the probability, under the null model and its assumptions, of a test statistic at least as extreme as observed. It is not the probability of the hypothesis. Biological importance needs the effect’s size, units, uncertainty, organism, and purpose. The test cannot repair dependent units.

title: Week 4 self-check — comparisons and fitted lines
section: 3. Pair by identity
text:
3. Pair by identity
The same ten plants were measured before and after increasing light. Why should the analysis use within-plant differences? Could independently sorting the two measurement columns improve their pairing?






Answer





The two readings belong to each same plant, so calculate after minus before within matching IDs. There are ten independent pairs, not twenty independent plants. Sorting columns independently destroys that identity and does not improve pairing. The fixed before/after order also leaves a time/order limitation.

title: Week 4 self-check — comparisons and fitted lines
section: 4. Invert the calibration in the stated direction
text:
4. Invert the calibration in the stated direction
The fitted line is approximately absorbance = 0.03957 + 0.06489 × concentration_mg_l. For an in-range absorbance of 0.310, what formula estimates concentration?






Worked answer





Rearrange to concentration = (0.310 - 0.03957) / 0.06489, giving about 4.17 mg/L. Use full fitted coefficients in code. We fitted absorbance as the measured response to known concentration; reversing the regression is a different fit. The inverse calculation is a point estimate, not full calibration uncertainty.

title: Week 4 self-check — comparisons and fitted lines
section: 5. A diluted reading is new evidence
text:
5. A diluted reading is new evidence
An unknown’s original reading is above the measured standards. Can you simply report the line’s extrapolated concentration? If a new in-range reading gives 7.40 mg/L after 1.00 mL was diluted to 10.00 mL total, what is the original estimate?






Answer and check





Flag the original as outside range rather than treat extrapolation as a supported result. A new in-range diluted measurement permits a stated correction: 7.40 × (10.00 / 1.00) ≈ 74.0 mg/L, using rounded numbers. The dilution assumes no measured material was lost or reacted. It does not validate another old out-of-range reading without its own new measurement.

title: Week 4 self-check — comparisons and fitted lines
section: 6. Slope units and causal limits
text:
6. Slope units and causal limits
A fitted dry-mass-versus-leaf-area slope is about 4.11. Dry mass is in mg and area in cm². What are the slope’s units, and what claim is not established by this observational fit?






Answer





The units are mg per cm²: fitted change in dry mass for a one-cm² increase in area. The sample association does not establish that experimentally changing area would cause this mass change. Inspect residuals and the measured range, and avoid extrapolating far beyond observed leaf areas.



Return to association practice, or continue to remote workflow.

title: Day 22 — a sequence is text; an image is numbers
text: Lecture slides · Weekly self-check

title: Day 22 — a sequence is text; an image is numbers
section: Today’s question
text:
Today’s question
Is a computer handling something fundamentally different when it stores a DNA sequence or a picture? The information has different meanings, but we can reuse familiar ideas: characters, numbers, vectors, tables, and saved files.
This is a short breadth session. We will not search a database, align sequences, or learn an image-analysis package. Allow time afterwards to practise earlier reports. Save today’s code as representations.R in the project root, and two or three explanatory sentences in reports/representations.txt.

title: Day 22 — a sequence is text; an image is numbers
section: 1. A DNA sequence as character data
text:
1. A DNA sequence as character data
At the storage level, files are sequences of bytes. A bit has two possible values, 0 or 1; a byte contains eight bits, giving 256 possible patterns. Software interprets those patterns using a format: they might encode text, brightness, or something else. The file extension helps applications choose how to read a file, but renaming photo.jpg to photo.csv does not convert its contents. We will interpret information through its format, not learn binary arithmetic.
DNA can be represented with letters A, C, G, and T. Our file is a tiny invented string, not a real gene. It is one line of plain text; the final newline separates lines in the file and is not an extra DNA base.
Run in R, with the course project open:
dna <- readLines("data/dna.txt")
dna
nchar(dna)
readLines() reads text lines; here it produces one character string. nchar() counts its characters. Compare with length(dna), which is 1: one stored string is different from forty separate character elements.
To count individual letters, split that string:
bases <- strsplit(dna, split = "")[[1]]
length(bases)
table(bases)
This new line is a supplied small example, not syntax to memorise. strsplit() returns a collection of results, one for each input string. [[1]] selects the first result. An empty split separates every character. table() then counts the occurrences of each different letter.
Try it: copy the printed sequence into a quoted R string, change one A to a G, and repeat the counts. Predict which counts change before running the code. Keep the supplied file unchanged. A total count of letters does not reveal what a sequence does in an organism; meaning needs biological context.






Hint: one string versus many letters





length(c("ACG", "TT")) is 2 because the vector has two strings. nchar(c("ACG", "TT")) gives 3 and 2. Ask which of these questions you want before interpreting a count.

title: Day 22 — a sequence is text; an image is numbers
section: 2. A small image as a table
text:
2. A small image as a table
A grayscale image can be stored as rows and columns of brightness values. Our deliberately tiny teaching image has eight rows and eight columns. On its 0–255 scale, 0 means black and 255 means white; it is not a measurement in mm. One byte can represent one intensity on that scale. The 64 intensities would need 64 bytes if stored directly as one byte each. Our CSV is larger because it stores the digits as text, plus commas, a header, and line endings. The same information can have different file sizes in different representations.
pixels <- as.matrix(read.csv("data/pixels.csv"))
dim(pixels)
pixels
pixels[1, 1]
pixels[4, 4]
read.csv() is used here to obtain a simple numeric table for the supplied matrix demonstration; ordinary course tables still use read_csv(). as.matrix() represents this all-numeric table as a rectangular matrix. pixels[4, 4] selects row 4, column 4. A pixel is a location in the image, not an independent organism.
To display the values, the following supplied code converts brightness to a 0–1 grayscale representation and draws it:
plot.new()
rasterImage(as.raster(pixels / 255), 0, 0, 1, 1)
The bright central object should be visible. The 0 and 1 coordinates specify the plotting region, not a calibrated physical scale. You cannot turn its pixel area into square millimetres without knowing the image calibration.

title: Day 22 — a sequence is text; an image is numbers
section: 3. Count a visibly defined region
text:
3. Count a visibly defined region
bright <- pixels > 100
bright
sum(bright)
mean(bright)
The comparison produces a matrix of TRUE/FALSE values. In a sum, R counts TRUE as 1 and FALSE as 0. mean(bright) is therefore the fraction of pixels above 100. We are reusing logical comparisons from table filtering. For this supplied image, 24 of 64 pixels are above 100: the fraction is 0.375.
Try it: compare thresholds 50, 100, and 220. Which pixels count as bright? Explain why this constructed two-level image is unusually easy to separate. Real microscope images may have noise, uneven lighting, and overlapping objects; a bright region is not automatically one cell.






Hint: a quick check without new syntax





Use sum(pixels > 50), then replace 50 with 100 and 220. The image contains only 25 and 210. Predict the outcome from these values before running each line.

title: Day 22 — a sequence is text; an image is numbers
section: Interpretation and limits
text:
Interpretation and limits
Write one sentence answering each question:

What is represented by a DNA character, a matrix cell, and a plant-table row?
What extra information would you need to call a bright area a cell?
Why is the number of pixels not an appropriate sample size for a test of a treatment applied to one plant?







Short answers





A DNA character represents a base label; a pixel cell represents brightness at a location; our plant-table row records measurements of one plant. Image interpretation needs acquisition context, scale, and biological validation. Pixels from one image are spatially related measurements, and one treated plant remains one experimental unit regardless of its number of pixels.



Before you finish: rerun representations.R from a fresh R session and save your explanatory notes. Next: a small integrated study.

title: Day 24 — can someone else render your report?
text: Lecture slides · Weekly self-check

title: Day 24 — can someone else render your report?
section: Today’s question
text:
Today’s question
A result that appears on your screen may depend on objects you created hours ago or a file stored outside your project. Today you will find those dependencies and produce a folder someone else can use. Reproducibility is a property you check by running the work, not an adjective you add to the title.
You need: yesterday’s .Rmd, its data, and your project folder. Save the revised report, its HTML, and a reports/reproduction-log.txt. A peer can help; if working alone, use a separately extracted copy and a fresh R session.
Use the study you selected on day 23. The folder example below uses duckweed; for the organic alternative, substitute organic-study.Rmd, its HTML, and data/organic-recovery.csv. Keep the data dictionary in either case. You only need to reproduce one report.

title: Day 24 — can someone else render your report?
section: 1. Close the gaps in the report
text:
1. Close the gaps in the report
Read the report as if you had not conducted the exercise. Does it identify the biological or laboratory question, simulated study design, independent units, data source, missing measurement, methods, and conclusion? Are figure axes and the comparison direction labelled? Can you distinguish SD among flasks from uncertainty in the estimated difference?
For the descriptive organic alternative, check SD among independent synthesis runs and the observed difference in percentage points. No test or confidence interval was required, so do not add one just to fill a report heading.
Replace notes such as “insert result here” with your interpretation. Keep enough code to reproduce the result. For this course, visible code is helpful; hiding code cannot correct a missing explanation.

title: Day 24 — can someone else render your report?
section: 2. Render after restarting
text:
2. Render after restarting
Save the .Rmd, restart R in RStudio, then use Knit without manually running analysis lines in the console first. Restarting removes session objects, while saved input files remain. If the render fails, locate the named chunk and read the first meaningful error before changing several things at once.








Failure
Likely dependency
Repair




object 'duckweed' not found
Import happened only in the console
Put import code before analysis chunks


A function is unavailable
Package was loaded only interactively
Add its library() call to setup


Input path cannot be opened
Personal absolute path or missing project files
Use data/duckweed.csv and include that file


Export fails
Destination directory was not included
Include the empty output folder or create it explicitly


Old text contradicts new numbers
Result was manually typed and not updated
Check interpretation and use inline results where useful



Do not add install.packages() to fix every render: software installation is separate setup. Tell the reader which packages are needed.

title: Day 24 — can someone else render your report?
section: 3. Package the necessary inputs and source
text:
3. Package the necessary inputs and source
Create a folder named report-share outside your working project using the file manager. Copy the following into it:
report-share/
├── introcomputing.Rproj
├── duckweed-report.Rmd
├── duckweed-report.html
├── README.txt
├── data/
│   ├── duckweed.csv
│   └── README.md
└── output/
    └── README.txt
Keep the data dictionary so the recipient knows the study design. The output folder is needed if the report explicitly saves a figure there. Exclude session files, credentials, and unrelated personal work. Write a short README stating that the data are simulated, required packages, the file to render, and the expected HTML output. The HTML alone is readable but is not the source analysis.
In a shell, from the folder containing report-share, make a ZIP:
zip -r report-share.zip report-share/
unzip -l report-share.zip
On Windows you may first use File Explorer to copy report-share into the Ubuntu shell workspace. Check its location before running the command. Native RStudio still uses the Windows copy. If you revise that Windows copy, copy the revised files into Ubuntu again before creating a replacement ZIP; the copies do not synchronise. Copy the finished ZIP back to a normal Windows folder before extracting it for the native RStudio check below. The archive should be outside the folder being archived; do not package a folder containing its own growing ZIP.

title: Day 24 — can someone else render your report?
section: 4. Reproduce from a different location
text:
4. Reproduce from a different location
Exchange the ZIP with a peer using the supported course sharing route. Extract it into a new folder, open its .Rproj, and render the .Rmd in a fresh R session. Do not silently fix the author’s source before trying it.
If working alone, rename the new parent folder so its path differs from the original. This checks that the report does not depend on a personal absolute path. A second folder on your own laptop checks portability, but does not fully test differences between software environments.
Compare the numerical results, group counts, and interpretation. Plot layout may vary slightly across software versions; a jitter seed helps point placement stay consistent. Record the software information if results differ:
sessionInfo()
You can put this in a report appendix or save its output in your log. You do not need to understand every entry: R version and loaded package versions help another person investigate a difference.






Hint: the project opens, but input is still missing





Look at the recipient’s actual extracted folder tree. A .Rproj file does not contain the data; it sets the project context. A shortcut to your original data folder is also not a transferred dataset. Include the ordinary CSV itself.

title: Day 24 — can someone else render your report?
section: What to record
text:
What to record
In reports/reproduction-log.txt, write the source archive name, destination folder, whether rendering succeeded before fixes, any exact error, the correction, and whether the rerun reproduced the key values. Thank your peer by making their feedback actionable, not by rating the appearance of their report.

title: Day 24 — can someone else render your report?
section: Check your understanding
text:
Check your understanding

Why can a report work after “Run All” but fail for a recipient?
Does a ZIP stored on the same disk protect against losing that disk?
What does a successful fresh-folder render establish?







Short answers






It may rely on session state, personal paths, or files not included in the ZIP.
No. A separate supported backup is needed for that failure.
That the supplied source and inputs can regenerate the report in the tested environment. It does not prove that the biological design or interpretation is correct, or that every future software version will behave identically.




Before you finish: retain the corrected report, tested ZIP, and a copy on the supported backup storage. Next: consolidation and error recovery.

title: Week 5 self-check — reproduce and transfer
text: Use these questions to check the whole workflow and locate any unfinished practical skills. They are not a graded test. Remote tasks requiring an account remain pending until the actual course service is provided.

title: Week 5 self-check — reproduce and transfer
section: 1. Name the location, not just the filename
text:
1. Name the location, not just the filename
Your report rendered remotely, but local Downloads is empty. What should you check? Does closing the SSH terminal necessarily delete saved remote output?






Answer





Locate the output on the remote computer, then check whether it was transferred and to which destination. A remote desktop is not automatic synchronisation. Closing SSH ends a session, not saved files, subject to the service’s storage policy. Do not assume a running process will continue after disconnecting.

title: Week 5 self-check — reproduce and transfer
section: 2. Count the represented thing
text:
2. Count the represented thing
dna <- readLines("data/dna.txt") reads one invented 40-letter line. What are length(dna) and nchar(dna)? Why do they differ?






Answer





length(dna) is 1 stored string; nchar(dna) is 40 characters in that string. Counting vector elements and counting characters answer different questions. The final newline in the file is not another DNA base.

title: Week 5 self-check — reproduce and transfer
section: 3. Pixels are positions, not plants
text:
3. Pixels are positions, not plants
The teaching image has 64 pixels, 24 above intensity 100. What fraction is bright? Does that make 64 independent biological replicates or identify one cell?






Answer





The fraction is 24/64 = 0.375. Pixels are related positions in one artificial image. Their count does not establish independent treatment replication or biological identity. Interpretation needs acquisition context, scale, and validation. The threshold count alone does not establish a cell’s area in mm².

title: Week 5 self-check — reproduce and transfer
section: 4. Available duckweed measurements
text:
4. Available duckweed measurements
Twenty independent flasks were started, ten per allocation. Nutrient flask F17 spilled before weighing. How many available biomass observations are there, and why is replacing the missing value by zero inappropriate?






Answer





There are 10 control and 9 nutrient observations, 19 in total. Zero would invent a known biomass; unavailable and absent biomass are different meanings. Retain the original row, report the loss, and make the comparison conditional on the observed data and missingness limitation.

title: Week 5 self-check — reproduce and transfer
section: 5. A percentage difference needs its units
text:
5. A percentage difference needs its units
In the supplied alternative, percentage yield is 100 × collected mass / supplied maximum mass, with matching mass units. Protocol means are 68.67% and 77.00%. Is their difference an 8.33% relative increase? Does it establish greater purity?






Answer





The modified-minus-standard difference is 8.33 percentage points. A relative percentage change would divide by the starting mean and multiply by 100; it is a different quantity. Greater yield alone does not establish greater purity, safety, sustainability, or general superiority. Product purity was an explicit simplifying assumption in this numerical exercise, not a measured finding.

title: Week 5 self-check — reproduce and transfer
section: 6. Share a recipe, not only its output
text:
6. Share a recipe, not only its output
A peer receives your HTML but cannot update the analysis for new data. What else should be in the shared project? Why test extraction in a new location?






Answer





Include the .Rmd source, actual input CSV, dictionary, project file, required output folder if used, and a short README naming packages and the file to render. Testing a new location detects dependencies on personal absolute paths or missing files. The .Rproj does not contain the dataset. A fresh session detects hidden interactive objects. Do not include credentials or unrelated personal work.

title: Week 5 self-check — reproduce and transfer
section: 7. What does successful reproduction establish?
text:
7. What does successful reproduction establish?
The peer renders your source successfully from the shared input. Does that prove the experimental design and interpretation are correct, or provide a backup against losing your only disk?






Answer





It establishes that the supplied work regenerates the result in the tested environment. A flawed analysis can be reproducible. Scientific validity still needs the design, assumptions, checks, and reasoning. Backup is a separate action: keep a retrievable copy using supported separate storage.



Return to day 25 consolidation and save your next-lab workflow with the reference pages.

title: Folders and the working computer
section: A project is a tree of locations
text:
A project is a tree of locations



A project parent folder contains data, output, and reports with their respective files.


data and reports are neighbours, not one inside the other.

Ask students to locate yesterday’s note first. Introduce parent folder and project root using the picture. Project root means the starting folder of this project, not the root of the entire computer. Have a student narrate the route from reports to data.

title: Folders and the working computer
section: An address can be absolute or relative
text:
An address can be absolute or relative
Example absolute path on Linux:
/home/anna/introcomputing-course/data/seedlings.csv
From the project root, the relative path is:
data/seedlings.csv
Your username and complete home path may differ.

Show Windows and Mac equivalents in the practical if needed. An absolute path supplies the full route from a drive or root. A relative path starts from the current folder. Do not have students copy the illustrative username; personal absolute paths are one reason analyses fail when moved.

title: Folders and the working computer
section: A relative path needs a starting point
text:
A relative path needs a starting point



The same relative path works from the project root but not from inside reports.


Current working directory: where relative paths start.

Physically move between the project root and reports in the graphical window. Say the route out loud. The file remains in data; changing the current folder changes the interpretation of a relative path. Tomorrow pwd will let a shell report this starting point.

title: Folders and the working computer
section: Opening a CSV uses several computer parts
text:
Opening a CSV uses several computer parts



Saved data are read from storage into working memory and processed by the CPU.


The operating system manages files, memory, devices, and running programs.

Link each component to an action: storage retains the CSV, RAM holds working information, CPU carries out instructions. RStudio will later be an application and a process will be a running instance of it. More RAM does not automatically mean more persistent room for photographs. Avoid hardware shopping or binary arithmetic.

title: Folders and the working computer
section: An unsaved change and a saved file differ
text:
An unsaved change and a saved file differ
Try this only on a practice note:

Add a sentence, save, close, and reopen.
Add another sentence and discard the change when closing.
Inspect the actual file after reopening.

If the editor restores unsaved state, discuss what it has restored.

The exercise reveals the difference between storage and current application state. Autosave changes the experience, so do not claim every editor behaves the same way. Ask the class where the saved note is and which sentence is actually stored there.

title: Folders and the working computer
section: Home folders belong to particular environments
text:
Home folders belong to particular environments



Laptop storage, local Ubuntu storage on Windows, and a remote Linux home are distinct file locations.


An explicit transfer or configured sharing is needed to connect separate copies.

Windows students use native RStudio and a separate Ubuntu shell. Mac students do not need local Ubuntu, but remote storage remains separate for them too. A cloud copy may synchronise, but a remote desktop is not automatically a sync service. The course’s actual remote connection details are pending.

title: Folders and the working computer
section: Which claim needs correcting?
text:
Which claim needs correcting?
“The note is in my editor, so I know where the file is.”
“I copied the ZIP beside the folder, so the laptop is backed up.”
“data/seedlings.csv means the same location from every folder.”

All need correction. The editor may be displaying an unsaved or recovered version; a same-disk ZIP does not protect against loss of that disk; relative paths need a starting folder. Ask for a concrete fix to each claim rather than vocabulary alone.

title: Folders and the working computer
section: Practise explaining the route
text:
Practise explaining the route
Open the practical and notes.
Save reports/day02-map.txt with:

A small project tree and the route to seedlings.csv.
One sentence distinguishing RAM from saved storage.
A note naming the computer holding your project.


The practical also creates practice/field-notes and figures for tomorrow’s navigation. Let pairs give directions without pointing or touching the other’s computer, then swap. Keep backup discussions tied to the supported storage route when it is announced.

title: Inspect laboratory data before calculating
section: Four samples, one manifest
text:
Four samples, one manifest



The supplied manifest contains one header and four sample records linked to measurement filenames.


This small simulated shell dataset is separate from the 24-plant R dataset.

Read a manifest as a list of what is present. IDs connect metadata to measurements. The file paths locate measurements, while the README supplies their meaning and units. Distinguish four sample records from five text lines before discussing any command count.

title: Inspect laboratory data before calculating
section: An archive is a package of files
text:
An archive is a package of files



Extracting lab-data.zip creates a folder of ordinary files while leaving the archive intact.


Copy the downloaded ZIP into the shell workspace deliberately.

On Windows the browser download is not automatically in Ubuntu. Open the shell workspace graphically and copy the file. On Mac use the same explicit location check. In a remote environment, use the provided transfer route; no login hostname is assumed here.

title: Inspect laboratory data before calculating
section: Inspect first; extract to a known destination
text:
Inspect first; extract to a known destination
unzip -l lab-data.zip
unzip lab-data.zip -d lab-data
cd lab-data
less README.txt
-l lists; -d names the extraction destination. Press q to leave less.

The archive has four measurement files and supporting notes. If extraction asks to overwrite, inspect the existing destination and choose a fresh folder rather than automatically replacing work. These commands do not remove the original ZIP. Keep the command sequence tied to the current working directory.

title: Inspect laboratory data before calculating
section: Text search selects matching lines
text:
Text search selects matching lines



Literal grep search highlights the S03 and S04 records containing treated.


grep -F treated samples.tsv

-F requests literal text matching. The prepared file has control and treated labels; its header does not include treated. Explain that untreated would also contain treated, so grep does not understand treatment allocation or table columns. Inspect selected lines before interpreting them.

title: Inspect laboratory data before calculating
section: A pipe connects the outputs and inputs
text:
A pipe connects the outputs and inputs



Four records enter a grep selection, two matching lines leave it, and wc counts two.


grep -F treated samples.tsv | wc -l

The pipe passes matching lines directly to the next program. wc -l counts newline-terminated lines, which represent records in this controlled file. No intermediate saved file is required. Ask students to predict 2 before running it, and compare with wc -l samples.tsv, which returns 5 including the header.

title: Inspect laboratory data before calculating
section: Redirection writes a separate output
text:
Redirection writes a separate output
grep -F treated samples.tsv > treated-samples.txt
less treated-samples.txt

The manifest is read; the extract is written.
> replaces existing contents at the destination.
Never use the input filename as this destination.


Students should explain which file changed. A text extract is not a full replacement manifest because it lacks the nonmatching header and control records. Show it in the file manager. Treat redirection as a concrete write action, not punctuation to memorise.

title: Inspect laboratory data before calculating
section: Work through one sample and one copy
text:
Work through one sample and one copy
head measurements/S03.csv
mkdir working
cp samples.tsv working/samples-copy.tsv
mv working/samples-copy.tsv working/manifest-practice.tsv
Which original files should still be present?

The original archive and manifest remain. Only the practice copy is renamed. The S03 measurement file has one observed length; find its units in README. cp and mv may replace a destination, so inspect the names before running. Ask students to identify S04’s path without copying the S03 line blindly.

title: Inspect laboratory data before calculating
section: Save an inspection someone can explain
text:
Save an inspection someone can explain
Open the practical and notes.
Keep the selected records, a practice manifest, and working/observations.txt.
Explain 5 lines, 4 samples, and 2 treated records in your own words.

The practical also introduces the local/remote distinction via a teacher demonstration when access is ready. If service accounts are pending, complete local file skills; do not invent a remote address or treat a local rehearsal as completed SSH access.

title: Let R keep track of the calculation
section: Ask which quantity you want
text:
Ask which quantity you want



The same plant is 20 mm initially and 37 mm finally; the increase is 17 mm.


Change is 37 - 20; the ratio 37 / 20 answers a different question.

Start from the simple biological question, not an overview of programming languages. All example plants are simulated. Growth has units of mm; a ratio of two lengths in the same units is dimensionless. Ask students to predict both before running R.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Let R keep track of the calculation
section: Assign a value to a name
text:
Assign a value to a name



An assigned object refers to a calculated value in memory, while the script stores instructions on disk.


Read <- as “store this under this name”.

The Environment pane shows current session objects; the editor shows saved instructions. Show that saving alone does not execute a line and executing alone does not save editor changes. An object does not remain available after an ordinary fresh session unless the instructions recreate it.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Let R keep track of the calculation
section: Write and run a small script
text:
Write and run a small script
Save as day06.R in the course project root:
initial_mm <- 20
final_mm <- 37
growth_mm <- final_mm - initial_mm
growth_mm
R names are case-sensitive: growth_mm differs from Growth_mm.

Open the extracted .Rproj first. Run each line using the editor’s Run action. Explain the unit-bearing names and comments rather than requiring one preferred naming convention. The Console prompt is not typed. If an object is missing, check spelling and the line that should create it.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Let R keep track of the calculation
section: Several values can share one object name
text:
Several values can share one object name



Three plant-specific pairs of initial and final measurements yield three matched growth values.


The order must refer to the same plants in both vectors.

Work through P02’s 40 minus 22 equals 18. The picture is positional arithmetic, not R automatically matching plant IDs. Later tables will preserve correspondence explicitly. Do not suggest that arbitrary equal-length vectors can be subtracted meaningfully.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Let R keep track of the calculation
section: Calculate, summarise, compare
text:
Calculate, summarise, compare
initial_mm <- c(20, 22, 19)
final_mm <- c(37, 40, 34)
growth_mm <- final_mm - initial_mm
mean(growth_mm)
length(growth_mm)
growth_mm > 16
Results: mean about 16.67 mm, length 3, comparison TRUE TRUE FALSE.

c combines values into a vector; mean and length are functions with parentheses. Greater-than gives logical values, not new measurements. Text needs quotation marks. Plant IDs are labels, so averaging them would not answer a useful question. Keep syntax explanations tied to these operations.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Let R keep track of the calculation
section: A ratio can describe product yield too
text:
A ratio can describe product yield too



Collected mass 0.62 g fills 62 percent of the supplied maximum product mass of 1.00 g.


Percentage yield = 100 × collected dry mass / supplied maximum mass.

This is the optional substitute for the extra plant-ratio exercise. Define synthesis as making a product; supply the theoretical mass without reaction balancing. Assume collected product is pure only for this calculation. Both masses use grams. Changing collected mass to 0.70 g gives 70%. A higher yield does not establish purity or safety.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Let R keep track of the calculation
section: Predict what survives a restart
text:
Predict what survives a restart
You have run the code but not saved the script. Then you restart R.

Which instructions are saved?
Which session objects must be recreated?
What should you run first after reopening?


The unsaved script changes may be lost or recoverable by the editor, but should not be relied upon. Save explicitly. In a fresh R session the objects need recreating from the beginning. Introduce error recovery as checking a dependency rather than running random lines until the error disappears. Esc cancels an unfinished expression marked by a plus prompt.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Let R keep track of the calculation
section: Practise a complete, repeatable calculation
text:
Practise a complete, repeatable calculation
Open the practical and notes.

Add a fourth plant to both measurement vectors.
Change an input, predict the effect, and rerun.
Save day06.R; restart and run it from the top.


The worked mean uses three plants; the practical then extends to four. Keep the input values and comments in the saved source so the result can be reconstructed. Students doing the organic ratio choice still practise the matched-plant vector basics.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Calculate a variable, then show the observations
section: Growth is a derived measurement
text:
Growth is a derived measurement



A growth column is derived from each plant’s final and initial measurements, preserving the original inputs.


For P01: 44.3 − 25.7 = 18.6 mm.

The raw file records two lengths. Growth is their difference for the same plant, not a change to the source CSV. Distinguish final size from growth: a plant can start larger and still grow less. A negative change deserves checking, not automatic deletion.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Calculate a variable, then show the observations
section: Add the column in code
text:
Add the column in code
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
seedlings <- read_csv("data/seedlings.csv",
                      show_col_types = FALSE)
seedlings <- mutate(seedlings,
                     growth_mm = final_mm - initial_mm)
Save the calculation in day08.R.

mutate returns a modified table that is assigned back to an object name. It finds the named columns in the supplied table. The packages must be loaded in this session. Ask students to inspect the new column and check P02’s growth, 8 mm, by hand.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Calculate a variable, then show the observations
section: Selecting rows is different from selecting columns
text:
Selecting rows is different from selecting columns



Highlighted treated rows are filtered, and then only ID and growth columns are selected.


filter() asks which observations? select() asks which variables?

Use control_plants <- filter(seedlings, treatment == “control”) and growth_table <- select(seedlings, plant_id, treatment, growth_mm) in the live demonstration. Explain that == compares while <- assigns. A pipe is a readable sequence of operations; it does not change their biological meaning.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Calculate a variable, then show the observations
section: Each plot answers a particular question
text:
Each plot answers a particular question



Actual simulated seedling data plotted with initial length on x and final length on y, coloured by allocation.


This shows final size against initial size, not growth against treatment.

Read the axes before discussing the pattern. Every point is a plant and colour is a group label. The plot is generated from the actual course CSV. It does not establish that starting larger causes a particular final size. The corresponding plotting code is in the practical.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Calculate a variable, then show the observations
section: Show growth for each plant
text:
Show growth for each plant



Individual seedling growth values overlap between the control and treated groups.


Horizontal jitter separates overlapping points; vertical values stay unchanged.

The practical’s position_jitter uses height = 0 and a seed for repeatable display. Ask the class what higher/lower means on this axis and whether the groups overlap. Do not declare a treatment effect solely from a plotted cloud; formal comparison and uncertainty come later.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Calculate a variable, then show the observations
section: A plot object and an image file differ
text:
A plot object and an image file differ
ggsave("output/seedling-growth.png",
       plot = growth_plot, width = 6, height = 4)
write_csv(growth_table, "output/seedling-growth.csv")
The output folder must exist. Locate the saved PNG and CSV in the file manager.

The code assumes growth_plot and growth_table have been created by the practical’s complete script. Naming a plot object does not save an image. An image does not contain the full source analysis. Both export operations can replace an existing destination, so use intentional names and keep raw inputs unchanged.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Calculate a variable, then show the observations
section: Transfer choice: percentage yield
text:
Transfer choice: percentage yield
For the optional organic-laboratory table, both masses are supplied in grams:
organic <- read_csv("data/organic-recovery.csv",
                   show_col_types = FALSE)
organic <- mutate(organic, yield_percent =
                    100 * isolated_mass_g / theoretical_mass_g)
Compare percentages when starting scales differ; a larger mass alone is insufficient.

Define theoretical mass as the supplied maximum and isolated mass as dry collected product assumed pure for this numerical task. No reaction equation is required. Y01 is 62%. This choice substitutes for an extra plant-plot variation, not the main seedling workflow. Higher yield does not establish higher purity or general protocol superiority.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Calculate a variable, then show the observations
section: Make a figure someone can read
text:
Make a figure someone can read
Open the practical and notes.

Use the intended table and columns.
Label axes with quantities and units.
Explain what one point represents and one limitation.
Save the source script, derived table, and figure.


Have students close and reopen the saved outputs, then rerun the script from a fresh session. A useful recovery question is whether a missing column was calculated earlier. Keep interpretation short and concrete; no new test or regression is needed in this lesson.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Your first biological report
section: Describe what was independently measured
text:
Describe what was independently measured



A schematic shows separate control and treated pots; the actual study has twelve independent plants per group.


The simulated study measures 24 plants twice, seven days apart.

This is a consolidation briefing, not another statistics lecture. Each plant has its own pot and a randomly allocated control/nutrient treatment. The nutrient formulation is unspecified. Two time measurements on the same plant are not two separate plants. Do not invent experimental details beyond the dictionary.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Your first biological report
section: Explain the method in biological terms
text:
Explain the method in biological terms
“Growth was calculated as final minus initial length for each plant, in mm.”
That explains more than “we called mutate()”.
The report still needs the import and calculation code so someone can rerun it.

Distinguish a scientific methods explanation from a transcript of function names. The reader should understand the operation without speaking R. Students already have working code from previous days; their job is to place it in a self-contained report and explain it.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Your first biological report
section: A readable figure shows the observations
text:
A readable figure shows the observations



Individual simulated growth measurements vary within both groups and overlap between allocations.


What is one dot? What does the vertical axis measure? Where is the overlap?

Expect one independently potted plant and change in length in mm. Ask for a concrete visible pattern and a limitation. Avoid p-values or an unsupported declaration that the treatment works. A mean across both groups would not answer whether groups differ; group summaries come next week.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Your first biological report
section: Connect evidence to an interpretation
text:
Connect evidence to an interpretation



A biological growth question leads to observations and then a written pattern with a stated limitation.


Say what you observe and what the observations alone cannot settle.

Possible prose: growth varied among plants in both groups, and treated values tended to be higher but overlapped controls. The small simulated sample and lack of a quantified uncertainty comparison limit conclusions. Do not prescribe a single identical sentence for everyone; ask what evidence supports their wording.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Your first biological report
section: Keep the project portable
text:
Keep the project portable



A whole project can move to another folder while retaining the relative route from report source to its data subfolder.


data/seedlings.csv should not contain your personal username.

The .Rmd stays at the project root. Generated HTML can be next to it or in the documented reports/ output folder. A project file sets a working context; it does not embed the data. The diagram motivates later peer reproduction without adding a new remote service procedure.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Your first biological report
section: Test it after restarting R
text:
Test it after restarting R
In the R Console, after saving first-report.Rmd:
rmarkdown::render("first-report.Rmd", output_dir = "reports")
If an object is missing, repair the source rather than hiding the gap in Console state.

Do not insert this render command into the report itself. Work from the first relevant error and its chunk. Check file paths, package loading, and the growth calculation before rewriting the whole report. A successful fresh-session render is evidence of reproducibility in this environment, not proof the interpretation is correct.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Your first biological report
section: Give the reader four short sections
text:
Give the reader four short sections
Open the practical and notes.

Question and data: design, measurements, independent unit.
Methods: import and growth calculation.
Results: a labelled figure and relevant calculated facts.
Interpretation: pattern, variation, and one limitation.


Save first-report.Rmd and its HTML. A partner should be able to read the HTML without RStudio and identify the units and meaning of a point. With spare practice time, the provided leaf-area/mass table offers a transfer exercise; it does not require fitting a line today. Keep time for support rather than extending the deck.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: An average is not every plant
section: Same average; different observations
text:
Same average; different observations



Two toy growth groups have the same 14 millimetre mean but different standard deviations.


What does the mean leave out?

Give students a moment to read the axis before naming SD. Both sets have mean 14 mm; one contains 13,14,15 and the other 8,14,20. The second set has greater spread. We need to describe centre and variation, not choose one number to represent all plants.

title: An average is not every plant
section: Mean and median describe a centre
text:
Mean and median describe a centre
x <- c(10, 10, 10, 100)
mean(x)       # 32.5
median(x)     # 10
The mean uses every value. The median is the middle of the ordered values.

For an even number of observations, the median averages the two middle values. The large observation changes the mean strongly; it does not make either function wrong. Check unusual values against source information rather than deleting them to make summaries agree.

title: An average is not every plant
section: Measure deviations from the mean
text:
Measure deviations from the mean



Growth values 12,14,16 have deviations minus 2,0,plus 2 millimetres from their mean.


Adding the signed deviations gives zero, even with spread.

Work through the three numbers slowly. Subtraction uses the same units as the measurement. Positive and negative deviations cancel. Squaring is one way to avoid cancellation and leads to the sample variance used by R.

title: An average is not every plant
