section: Variance has squared units; SD has the original units
text:
Variance has squared units; SD has the original units



A two millimetre deviation squared corresponds to four square millimetres.


For 12, 14, 16: variance = 4 mm², SD = 2 mm.

The sum of squared deviations is 4+0+4=8. Divide by n−1=2 for sample variance, giving 4 mm². The square root is 2 mm. Explain the denominator as a sample-variance convention that estimates population variance; no derivation is needed. SD is not an error bar for the mean.

title: An average is not every plant
section: Let R do the arithmetic, while you keep the meaning
text:
Let R do the arithmetic, while you keep the meaning
x <- c(12, 14, 16)
mean(x)
var(x)
sd(x)
A mean or SD needs its measurement unit in the report.

Ask students to predict 14,4,2 before running. Their task is not memorising function names: it is choosing the quantity that answers their question and labelling the output correctly. Neither SD nor variance means every observation lies within a specified range.

title: An average is not every plant
section: Our control plants vary around their mean
text:
Our control plants vary around their mean



Individual control growth values and their 15.275 millimetre mean are shown on one axis.


Mean ≈ 15.28 mm; sample SD ≈ 3.19 mm.

These are the complete clean seedling data, not yesterday’s deliberately incomplete export. State the switch explicitly:12 control plants now contribute. The mean is a summary, not an observed “average plant”. Biological and measurement variation may both contribute to spread.

title: An average is not every plant
section: Changing the origin is different from changing the unit
text:
Changing the origin is different from changing the unit



Adding a constant shifts the mean; converting millimetres to centimetres changes the numeric scale.


Predict what happens to SD before running R.

Adding 10 mm changes 13,14,15 into 23,24,25: mean shifts from 14 to 24, SD remains 1 mm. Dividing by 10 gives 1.3,1.4,1.5 cm: mean 1.4 cm and SD 0.1 cm. Variance divides by 100. This is a units check, not a new statistical method.

title: An average is not every plant
section: Transfer choice: a yield is a percentage
text:
Transfer choice: a yield is a percentage
A supplied maximum is 1.00 g; collected dry product is 0.62 g.
yield_percent = 100 × collected mass / supplied maximum mass

Yield = 62%; no reaction equation is needed.
SD of several yields is in percentage points.
A higher yield alone does not establish higher purity.


This is an alternative small task, not additional compulsory work. Theoretical maximum masses are supplied in organic-recovery.csv. Collected dry material is assumed pure for this simplified calculation. Across six standard runs mean yield is 68.67% and SD 4.32 percentage points. Distinguish a percentage scale from relative percentage change.

title: An average is not every plant
section: Practical: explain the number you calculate
text:
Practical: explain the number you calculate
Choose one short transfer task and keep day12-variation.R.
What would stay the same if every measurement increased by 10 mm?
What changes when mm become cm?
Open the practical and answer checks.

Keep the by-hand three-number example before the full dataset. Ask for a two-sentence explanation of centre and spread. Students should retain the measurement unit and recognise that SD among plants is not uncertainty in a treatment difference.

title: What counts as independent evidence?
section: What received its own treatment allocation?
text:
What received its own treatment allocation?



Twelve separate pots illustrate individual plants as independently allocated units.


In our seedling study, the pot/plant is the experimental unit.

The picture illustrates separate pots, but physical separation alone is not proof of independence. The design description specifies independent allocation and handling. Ask students which entity could receive control while another receives treatment.

title: What counts as independent evidence?
section: More readings can still mean one plant
text:
More readings can still mean one plant



Six separate ruler readings all refer to the same plant P01.


Technical repeats help describe measurement variation.

Rereading the same plant may reveal consistency of the measurement process. It does not create new independently allocated plants or evidence about how different plants respond. The organic analogue is repeatedly weighing one collected product batch.

title: What counts as independent evidence?
section: A shared treatment can make the tray the unit
text:
A shared treatment can make the tray the unit



Plants grouped within two trays share one treatment per tray.


Do not count every plant as independently assigned.

This is a schematic layout, not the actual course experiment. If treatment was assigned once to each tray, plants within that tray share its allocation and environment. Ask how many treatment assignments occurred, not how many measurements fill the spreadsheet.

title: What counts as independent evidence?
section: SD among plants and uncertainty in a mean differ
text:
SD among plants and uncertainty in a mean differ
Spread: how much individual plants vary.
Sampling uncertainty: how much our mean would vary across repeated samples.
A larger independent sample can stabilise its mean without making plants identical.

A group SD and a standard error answer different questions. Larger sample size does not make the underlying biological distribution narrower. Repeated dependent observations do not necessarily provide the information gain promised by more independent samples.

title: What counts as independent evidence?
section: Each point in a sampling distribution is a mean
text:
Each point in a sampling distribution is a mean



Means of sixteen simulated draws cluster more tightly than means of four draws from the same toy distribution.


The source values stay fixed.

The supplied R demonstration uses the combined growth values as a fixed toy population and samples with replacement. It is not a new treatment experiment or a claim about nature. Each histogram entry summarises one simulated sample, not one freshly measured plant.

title: What counts as independent evidence?
section: Read the horizontal axis before comparing spread
text:
Read the horizontal axis before comparing spread



Individual growth values,means of four draws,and means of sixteen draws are distinct distributions.


Individual values and estimated means are different objects.

This additional picture is regenerated from the course values using a fixed illustrative random generator; exact bins need not match the R demonstration. The concept is the narrower distribution of larger-sample means. Do not interpret SD of means as SD among plants within a sample.

title: What counts as independent evidence?
section: Run the supplied demonstration; do not write a simulator
text:
Run the supplied demonstration; do not write a simulator
set.seed(14)
means_4 <- replicate(400,
  mean(sample(population_mm, size = 4, replace = TRUE)))
means_16 <- replicate(400,
  mean(sample(population_mm, size = 16, replace = TRUE)))
set.seed() makes the random demonstration repeatable.

The practical imports and defines population_mm before these lines. Explain sample as drawing values, replace=TRUE as allowing a source value again, and replicate as repeating the calculation. Students predict and interpret the result; functions and loops are not a new programming requirement.

title: What counts as independent evidence?
section: A stable estimate can still answer the wrong question
text:
A stable estimate can still answer the wrong question
If one unrepresentative tray is measured very precisely, have we learned the population mean accurately?
Which problem would another ruler reading fix?
Which problem needs another independently chosen unit?

Precision does not remove bias, dependence, or unrepresentative sampling. Another reading may help measurement consistency; another independently allocated or sampled unit addresses a different uncertainty. Avoid claiming that sample size alone guarantees a valid study.

title: What counts as independent evidence?
section: Practical: draw the design and explain the mean
text:
Practical: draw the design and explain the mean
Label independently treated units in three designs.
Run the supplied sampling demonstration and explain the axis.
Keep your diagrams and day14-sampling.R.
Open the practical.

Protect time for diagrams and discussion. The organic diagram can substitute for one plant example, not add another simulation. A useful explanation identifies what was repeated, what remained the same, and what increased the independent information.

title: What difference are we estimating?
section: Does nutrient allocation change seven-day growth?
text:
Does nutrient allocation change seven-day growth?



Twelve controls and twelve treated seedlings represent independent pot allocations.


Name the question, outcome, units, and independently allocated unit.

The course data are simulated. The study description supplies the random-allocation assumption; row order does not prove it. Growth is final minus initial length in millimetres. There are 12 plants per group, measured twice but contributing one growth value each.

title: What difference are we estimating?
section: Start with the observations
text:
Start with the observations



Individual plants show overlap and different group locations in growth.


A group mean does not describe every plant.

Ask students what a dot represents and whether any value obviously contradicts the documented measurement process. There is no known source error in this complete table. Do not remove values simply because they reduce a group difference.

title: What difference are we estimating?
section: State the direction before calculating
text:
State the direction before calculating



The treated mean exceeds the control mean by about 6.22 millimetres.


Treated minus control is our reported difference.

Control mean 15.275 mm, treated mean 21.49167 mm, difference 6.21667 mm. Reversing subtraction changes the sign without changing the observed experiment. A reader needs the direction and units to interpret an estimate.

title: What difference are we estimating?
section: One change per independently treated plant
text:
One change per independently treated plant
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
seedlings <- read_csv("data/seedlings.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(growth_mm = final_mm - initial_mm)
treated <- seedlings |> filter(treatment == "treated") |> pull(growth_mm)
control <- seedlings |> filter(treatment == "control") |> pull(growth_mm)
mean(treated) - mean(control)
Keep this preparation in comparison.Rmd.

Load readr, dplyr, ggplot2 before these lines, as in the practical. pull extracts the numeric column. These objects are vectors here, not the full group tables. Tomorrow’s lecture and test use exactly these definitions and direction.

title: What difference are we estimating?
section: Paired observations require a real identity
text:
Paired observations require a real identity



Different plants form independent groups; the same plant measured twice forms a pair.


Two columns or two labels alone do not establish pairing.

Today compares separate plants. Later, the same plant measured before and after a light change will require within-plant matching. Do not pair unrelated plants merely because their rows happen to align.

title: What difference are we estimating?
section: Do we have plants or shared treatment units?
text:
Do we have plants or shared treatment units?



A tray-wide allocation creates shared treatment units even when many plants are measured.


The design determines whether the group comparison is justified.

Revisit the replication concept before running inference. The shown tray layout is a counterexample, not the course study. One tray per treatment would not provide twelve independent treatment assignments per group. A function cannot repair that limitation.

title: What difference are we estimating?
section: Size of an effect and variability are separate questions
text:
Size of an effect and variability are separate questions
The sample difference is about 6.22 mm.
The group SDs describe how much plants vary within each group.
Tomorrow we estimate uncertainty in the population mean difference.

Do not use the two within-group SDs as if they were a confidence interval for the difference. Variation among measurements is the starting information for uncertainty, but the quantities answer different questions. Avoid introducing an extra formula today.

title: What difference are we estimating?
section: What might weaken the interpretation?
text:
What might weaken the interpretation?

Non-independent units or biased allocation.
Recording mistakes or a dominant questionable observation.
A small sample with severe skew.
An outcome that does not answer the biological question.


This list guides inspection, not a mechanical test-selection algorithm. For this introductory example the supplied design supports independent groups. If an actual practical looks unsuitable, seeking advice is a successful outcome; deleting genuine observations until a test works is not.

title: What difference are we estimating?
section: Practical: prepare before testing
text:
Practical: prepare before testing
Create comparison.Rmd with design, growth calculation, observations, and the directed difference.
Explain why the two groups are independent.
Open the practical.

Ask students to read their difference aloud with units and direction. Tomorrow the report gains an interval and p-value; today’s work should already be scientifically intelligible without either.

title: The same plant measured twice
section: Which two readings belong together?
text:
Which two readings belong together?



Plant IDs connect before and after observations even when their row order differs.


Pair by identity, not accidental row position.

The file paired.csv stores one plant per row with both readings, so matching is preserved. The diagram imagines two differently ordered lists to make the identity principle visible. Students do not need a join operation for this practical; they need to recognise that labels carry meaning.

title: The same plant measured twice
section: Read the within-plant paths
text:
Read the within-plant paths



Each of ten independent plants connects its before and after photosynthesis readings.


Ten plants, ten pairs; not twenty independent plants.

Photosynthesis rate is measured in micromoles CO2 per square metre per second. Each line links one plant’s non-destructive reading before and after increasing illumination. The prepared data show positive changes for every plant, but other datasets could have mixed directions.

title: The same plant measured twice
section: Subtract within each plant first
text:
Subtract within each plant first



Three example plants show their after-minus-before change on the original measurement scale.


Positive change means the measured rate increased.

L01 changes 6.95−5.87=1.08; L02 changes 11.92−7.75=4.17; L03 changes 10.12−8.81=1.31. These examples show why pairing concerns each plant’s change, not merely comparing two unlabelled collections of readings.

title: The same plant measured twice
section: One paired comparison in R
text:
One paired comparison in R
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
paired_data <- read_csv("data/paired.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
paired_data <- paired_data |>
  mutate(change = after_umol_m2_s - before_umol_m2_s)
paired_comparison <- t.test(
  paired_data$after_umol_m2_s, paired_data$before_umol_m2_s,
  paired = TRUE)
After minus before is the direction of the result.

Load readr and dplyr first in the report. The paired argument tells t.test that each position in the first vector belongs with the corresponding position in the second. Keeping both readings in one ID-checked table prevents independent sorting. This is not a method for pairing arbitrary groups.

title: The same plant measured twice
section: Changes differ among plants
text:
Changes differ among plants



The ten within-plant changes are plotted against plant identifiers.


Mean change ≈ 1.983 µmol CO₂ m⁻² s⁻¹.

The y-axis is the difference, not the after reading. Its zero line means no recorded within-plant change. L02 has a larger change than several others; this alone is not a recording error. The mean change and its uncertainty use 10 independent pairs.

title: The same plant measured twice
section: Pairing changes the information used
text:
Pairing changes the information used
A paired comparison asks whether the mean within-plant change is zero.
A one-sample comparison of those changes gives the same result:
t.test(paired_data$change, mu = 0)
Do not independently sort the before and after columns.

This equivalence supports understanding, not a demand to learn another method. The subject-to-subject differences in starting level are accounted for through within-subject subtraction. Pairing must be justified by design, and the pairs still need to be independent of one another.

title: The same plant measured twice
section: The design has a limit the test cannot remove
text:
The design has a limit the test cannot remove



The study changes light condition while time passes between the before and after readings.


No unchanged-light group; the same order was used for every plant.

We observe a change after the procedure, but light, elapsed time and measurement order accompany one another. The paired t-test does not separate them. Do not claim that a small p-value proves light alone caused the change.

title: The same plant measured twice
section: Report change, uncertainty, and the ordering limit
text:
Report change, uncertainty, and the ordering limit
Mean after-minus-before change: 1.983 µmol CO₂ m⁻² s⁻¹.
95% CI: 1.255 to 2.711; paired two-sided p ≈ 0.000166.
These describe a change under the study conditions, not an isolated light effect.

The confidence interval concerns the population mean change, under the assumptions. It does not describe the range of most plants’ individual changes. Sensible precision and a direct order/time limitation matter more than copying every decimal from the console.

title: The same plant measured twice
section: Practical: keep the pair visible
text:
Practical: keep the pair visible
Make paired-report.Rmd with the design, matched changes, a figure, result, and limitation.
Could a reader identify what counted as one independent pair?
Open the practical.

Check the practical’s chosen source report filename and use its code from the top. Ask students to explain why two unrelated groups cannot become paired by putting them beside one another. No new biology or chemical prerequisite is needed.

title: A line through biological measurements
section: Do larger leaves tend to have greater dry mass?
text:
Do larger leaves tend to have greater dry mass?



Leaves from different plants illustrate measured area and mass without any assigned treatment.


One leaf from each of 18 independent plants.

This is an observational dataset. We measured area and dry mass, not experimentally changed one while holding everything else fixed. One leaf per plant supplies the independent unit for this introductory example. The illustrated leaves are schematic; the plots use the actual course CSV.

title: A line through biological measurements
section: Start by plotting the measured variables
text:
Start by plotting the measured variables



Leaf area and dry mass form a positive observed association with a fitted line.


Horizontal: area (cm²). Vertical: dry mass (mg).

Ask students to read the axes before describing the trend. These are not the calibration standards from yesterday, and neither variable was assigned experimentally. The line summarises the observed association; scatter around it matters.

title: A line through biological measurements
section: Fit the same simple kind of model
text:
Fit the same simple kind of model
library(readr)
leaves <- read_csv("data/leaf-mass.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
leaf_fit <- lm(dry_mass_mg ~ leaf_area_cm2, data = leaves)
coef(leaf_fit)
Fitted mass ≈ 9.48 + 4.11 × area.

The input columns and units differ, but the lm syntax is the same as calibration. Intercept is about 9.476606 mg; slope about 4.110117 mg per cm². The intercept locates the line at area 0, outside the observed area range; do not interpret it as measured mass of a zero-area leaf.

title: A line through biological measurements
section: The slope has units
text:
The slope has units



A one-square-centimetre step along the fitted line corresponds to about 4.11 milligrams in fitted mass.


Slope ≈ 4.11 mg per cm².

We say the fitted mass is 4.11 mg greater for a one cm² increase in area within this descriptive model. That does not establish what would happen under an intervention. The red step shows the line’s change, not a measured before/after change in a particular leaf.

title: A line through biological measurements
section: Use the line inside the observed range
text:
Use the line inside the observed range
At area 8 cm²:
9.476606 + 4.110117 × 8 ≈ 42.36 mg
This is a fitted mean relationship, not the exact mass of every leaf that size.

Use the stored unrounded coefficients in actual calculations. The point prediction has uncertainty and individuals scatter around the line. Full regression inference is deferred. Here the point 8 cm² lies within the observed 2.96–14.68 cm² area range.

title: A line through biological measurements
section: Residuals keep the scatter visible
text:
Residuals keep the scatter visible



Residuals show observed mass minus fitted mass across measured leaf areas.


Residuals are in milligrams, the outcome’s units.

A positive residual means heavier than fitted at that area. Look for structure or a dominating point while remembering that small samples provide limited diagnostics. The line need not explain every biological difference. We do not teach a formal normality-test decision tree.

title: A line through biological measurements
section: Investigate influence without deleting inconvenient data
text:
Investigate influence without deleting inconvenient data



The full fit is compared with a labelled sensitivity fit omitting A18.


A18 is not a known recording error.

The default result retains all 18 plants. A labelled sensitivity check can reveal whether a conclusion depends strongly on one point. Omitting A18 gives a slightly different slope, about 4.064927 mg per cm². This is an illustration of influence, not permission to choose whichever subset yields the preferred result.

title: A line through biological measurements
section: An extended line is not extended evidence
text:
An extended line is not extended evidence



The observed leaf-area range is separated from a dashed unsupported extension.


No measurements support the shaded region.

The dashed extension is deliberately drawn as a warning. A formula produces a number at 25 cm², but there are no such observations here and the relationship may change. Distinguish arithmetic from evidence. The same range principle applied to assay calibration.

title: A line through biological measurements
section: Association does not establish an intervention effect
text:
Association does not establish an intervention effect
“Larger leaves tended to have greater dry mass in this sample.”
This does not prove that forcing area to increase would cause the fitted mass change.
Plant age, species, growing conditions, and other properties may vary together.

The named possible factors are examples of missing context, not measured covariates to add to a model. We are not introducing multiple regression or causal adjustment. The outcome is a restrained interpretation of an observational pattern.

title: A line through biological measurements
section: Practical: explain the line, the residuals, and one limit
text:
Practical: explain the line, the residuals, and one limit
Create association-report.Rmd with observations, fitted line, slope units, and residuals.
Keep the full-data result and label any sensitivity check.
Open the practical.

Check the exact source filename in the practical; use the root project convention. Ask students to choose one actual point and explain its residual sign. Their final report should distinguish descriptive association, supported range and a causal claim.

title: Text, pixels, and measurements
section: Different meanings, familiar representations
text:
Different meanings, familiar representations



DNA text, image pixels, and a plant observation illustrate three kinds of stored information.


Our task: identify what each stored value represents.

This is a short breadth session using invented DNA and an artificial image. We are not introducing a sequence-analysis or image-processing pipeline. Students can transfer vectors, tables, logical comparisons, and interpretation.

title: Text, pixels, and measurements
section: A file format gives bytes meaning
text:
A file format gives bytes meaning



Eight bits form a byte with 256 possible patterns.


Renaming photo.jpg to photo.csv does not convert the contents.

A bit has two possible values; eight bits yield 256 patterns. We do not need binary arithmetic. One format may use a byte for brightness; another uses encoded characters. The extension helps an application choose how to read it.

title: Text, pixels, and measurements
section: One string is not forty vector elements
text:
One string is not forty vector elements
dna <- readLines("data/dna.txt")
length(dna)  # 1 stored string
nchar(dna)   # 40 characters in that string
length() and nchar() answer different questions.
bases <- strsplit(dna, split = "")[[1]]
length(bases)  # 40 separate letters

Run from the course project. The final newline is not another DNA base. strsplit returns a collection of results, and [[1]] selects the first. Supply this code rather than requiring list syntax as a new programming outcome.

title: Text, pixels, and measurements
section: Counts describe this invented sequence
text:
Counts describe this invented sequence



Counts from the supplied sequence: A11, C9, G9, T11.


table(bases) counts letters; it does not reveal a gene’s biological function.

Ask students to predict the result of replacing one A by a G. A falls by one, G increases by one, and the total remains forty. Preserve the source file and change an R object for this experiment. Meaning requires biological context.

title: Text, pixels, and measurements
section: An image can be a rectangular numeric table
text:
An image can be a rectangular numeric table



The supplied 8 by 8 intensity table and the same values displayed as grayscale.


0 means black; 255 means white on this teaching scale.

The source image has only values 25 and 210. One byte could store each intensity, but the CSV uses text digits plus delimiters and a header. The 64 values need not occupy only 64 bytes in that representation. No physical scale is provided.

title: Text, pixels, and measurements
section: A threshold is a stated comparison
text:
A threshold is a stated comparison



An intensity threshold of 100 selects 24 pixels; 220 selects none.


Changing a threshold changes the question we ask of the same values.

Both images come from the actual supplied matrix. Because this constructed image has only two levels, separating its centre is unusually easy. Noise, lighting, and overlapping real objects would complicate interpretation.

title: Text, pixels, and measurements
section: Reuse logical values to count
text:
Reuse logical values to count
pixels <- as.matrix(read.csv("data/pixels.csv"))
bright <- pixels > 100
sum(bright)   # 24
mean(bright)  # 0.375
TRUE contributes 1 and FALSE contributes 0.
The fraction is 24 / 64, not 24 independent organisms.

Here read.csv plus as.matrix supplies a simple numeric matrix. Normal biological tables still use read_csv. The calculation counts qualifying pixels; it has not identified cells or calibrated area in square millimetres.

title: Text, pixels, and measurements
section: A pixel is not an experimental replicate
text:
A pixel is not an experimental replicate

An image position holds one brightness value.
Many positions can belong to one plant or one field of view.
A treatment assigned to one plant still has one treated plant.

What extra information would you need to interpret the bright object biologically?

Possible answers: acquisition context, physical scale, what was imaged, biological validation, and how treatment was assigned. Relate this to technical measurements and independent units from day 14, rather than introducing another test.

title: Text, pixels, and measurements
section: Prediction before code
text:
Prediction before code
Our only pixel values are 25 and 210.
What do these comparisons count?
sum(pixels > 50)
sum(pixels > 100)
sum(pixels > 220)

Ask before running: 24, 24, 0. A change in a threshold need not always change the count; it depends on which values occur. The threshold alone does not define a cell or specify physical area.

title: Text, pixels, and measurements
section: Practical: explain the representation
text:
Practical: explain the representation
Open day 22 practical and notes.

Save representations.R and short interpretation notes.
Reuse supplied code; focus on what its values and counts mean.
Keep original files intact and rerun from a fresh session.

Use remaining time to consolidate earlier reports.

Keep this breadth activity short. It should build confidence in transferable ideas, not become a third specialist software unit.

title: Can someone else reproduce it?
section: Your screen may contain hidden prerequisites
text:
Your screen may contain hidden prerequisites



An interactive R object does not automatically become part of a saved report.


“It works on my screen” is a starting observation, not a reproduction check.

An imported object can remain in interactive memory while its import is missing from the report. The recipient lacks that session. Do not add machinery such as saving an entire workspace; put the needed imports and calculations in the source.

title: Can someone else reproduce it?
section: Source and result have different jobs
text:
Source and result have different jobs



Input data and R Markdown source produce an HTML result.


HTML is readable. .Rmd plus inputs makes the analysis repeatable.

An HTML output does not by itself supply the original analysis recipe. Ask students which file they would edit when new measurements arrive and which they would send for someone simply to read.

title: Can someone else reproduce it?
section: Restart, then render from saved files
text:
Restart, then render from saved files

Save the source .Rmd.
Restart R.
Knit without manually recreating console objects first.
Read the first meaningful error and named chunk, if rendering stops.

Keep software installation separate from every report render.

The source should load its packages, import input files, and create all its objects. Restarting does not delete saved data files. If students use a Console render command, it belongs outside the report: a report must not render itself.

title: Can someone else reproduce it?
section: A recipient needs the whole small project
text:
A recipient needs the whole small project



The share folder includes a project file, report source, data and dictionary, output, and README.


Use the selected study’s source and CSV; the .Rproj does not contain them.

For duckweed use duckweed-report.Rmd and data/duckweed.csv. For the organic alternative use organic-study.Rmd and data/organic-recovery.csv. Include the dictionary and required output directory. A shortcut to the author’s files is not a transferred dataset.

title: Can someone else reproduce it?
section: Copies do not update themselves
text:
Copies do not update themselves



Windows and Ubuntu hold separately copied folders; edits must be recopied before packaging.


Revised source → recopy → repackage → test the returned ZIP.

This is especially important for Windows students using Ubuntu shell tools but native RStudio. After making a ZIP in Ubuntu, copy it back to a normal Windows folder for extraction and the native application test. Do not accidentally test stale files or rely on WSL paths in the shared report.

title: Can someone else reproduce it?
section: Test in a different location
text:
Test in a different location



A complete project is zipped and extracted into a fresh location before rendering.


Open its .Rproj, restart, and render the source without repairing it first.

Peer exchange tests a recipient’s environment. A fresh folder on the same laptop checks portability but not all software differences. Keeping the relative data/ path tests that the analysis does not rely on an author’s personal path.

title: Can someone else reproduce it?
section: Diagnose one dependency at a time
text:
Diagnose one dependency at a time







Symptom
First check




Object not found
Was it created inside the report, before use?


Function unavailable
Is its package loaded in setup?


Cannot open data
Which computer, project, and relative path?


Export directory missing
Include or explicitly create the destination.




Ask students to reproduce the exact failure before changing multiple things. The error identifies a question to investigate; it does not always identify the full cause. Credentials never belong in an error log or screenshot.

title: Can someone else reproduce it?
section: Review meaning as well as execution
text:
Review meaning as well as execution

What is the question and independent unit?
Are axes, counts, units, and comparison direction clear?
Does the prose agree with the actual results?
Are missing data and limitations explained?

For a descriptive organic report, do not invent a test or confidence interval.

A successful render can reproduce a mistaken analysis. Ask the reader to locate evidence for the conclusions, not just confirm that an HTML file exists.

title: Can someone else reproduce it?
section: A successful rerun is a bounded claim
text:
A successful rerun is a bounded claim
It establishes that the supplied source and inputs regenerate the result in the tested environment.
It does not establish:

Correct biological design or interpretation.
Compatibility with every future software version.
Protection against losing the only storage device.


Distinguish reproduction, scientific validity, and backup. Use sessionInfo when investigating software-version differences, without expecting beginners to interpret every field. A ZIP beside the original is not a separate backup.

title: Can someone else reproduce it?
section: Practical: keep a reproduction log
text:
Practical: keep a reproduction log
Open day 24 practical and notes.

Produce one tested share ZIP and corrected report.
Record destination, first error, fix, and rerun outcome.
Retain source, input, HTML, and a supported backup copy.

Use the study you chose yesterday.

Feedback should identify actions another person can reproduce. Keep this as formative practice, not a report-grading exercise. A fresh render is the endpoint.
